question_text: A 43-year-old woman with ESRD comes because of pain in her extremities. Serum calcium is 7.8 mg/dL, and parathyroid hormone levels (iPTH) are 370 pg/mL (normal by this assay = 10 - 60 pg/mL). Calcium-containing phosphate binders and vitamin D are administered until the patient's serum calcium reaches 8.4 mg/dL. At this point, the physician prescribes a drug to treat the patient's osteolysis. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of this drug?
option_a: Competitive antagonist of the aldosterone receptor
option_b: Increases sensitivity of the calcium-sensing receptor
option_c: Inhibits NaCI reabsorption in the early distal convoluted tubule
option_d: The Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>/CIT cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
explanation:
• This patient with end-stage renal disease has developed secondary hyperparathyroidism. The damaged kidneys do not excrete phosphate well, and the phosphate tends to precipitate with calcium, leading to hypocalcaemia. Hypocalcemia stimulates hyperplasia of the parathyroid glands, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism. The increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels partially restore the calcium levels toward normal; if the calcium levels overshoot to cause hypercalcemia, the patient is considered to have tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
    • The primary therapeutic goals of the treatment of secondary hyperparathyroidism are to decrease the levels of PTH and phosphorus in the blood. In patients with chronic kidney disease who are on dialysis, a decrease in PTH is associated with a positive impact on bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BALP), bone turnover, and bone fibrosis.
    • Cinacalcet is a calcimimetic agent that increases the sensitivity of the calcium- sensing receptor (CaSR) on chief cells of the parathyroid gland to extracellular calcium. This causes a reduction in PTH. Cinacalcet is indicated for the management of secondary hyperparathyroidism in patients with chronic kidney disease (and parathyroid level, iPTH >300 pg/mL) and for the treatment of hypercalcemia in patients with parathyroid carcinoma. With cinacalcet, the target is to maintain iPTH within the range of 150 - 300 pg/mL in dialysis patients.
    • Additional therapeutic options include dietary restriction of phosphorus, the use of phosphate binders (e.g., sevelamer, aluminum hydroxide, calcium salts), and administration of vitamin D and its derivatives. Surgery is generally indicated in patients with excessively elevated parathyroid hormone levels (>800 pg/mL) and/or patients who fail to respond to treatment with pharmacologic therapies.
    • Note that cinacalcet should not be administered if calcium levels are below normal; this is the rationale for the administration of the calcium-containing phosphate binders and vitamin D.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 793

question_text: A 45-year-old man goiter undergoes a thyroidectomy. One week later, he develops carpopedal spasms, muscle and abdominal cramps, and tingling of his lips and hands. Laboratory studies show a serum calcium of 6.2 mg/dL and serum phosphorus of 5.7 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs will most likely improve this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
• This patient is presenting with signs and symptoms highly suggestive of hypoparathyroidism, a condition that occurs most frequently after thyroidectomy or the removal of a parathyroid adenoma. Hypoparathyroidism is a condition of parathyroid hormone (PTH) deficiency leading to decreased calcium levels and other electrolyte abnormalities.
  • Normally a fall in extracellular fluid ionized calcium concentration leads to stimulation of PTH secretion. When released, PTH enhances active reabsorption of calcium and magnesium from distal tubules and the thick ascending limb in the kidney, enhances the release of calcium from bones and enhances the absorption of calcium in the intestine by increasing the production of activated vitamin D. However, in hypoparathyroidism, PTH levels are greatly reduced resulting in severe hypocalcemia.
  • There are three principal reasons for low Ca2+ in such cases
    • Low PTH reduces renal reabsorption of Ca++ but increases reabsorption of phosphate.
    • The resulting high plasma phosphate binds plasma Ca++ so plasma Ca++ decreases.
    • Low PTH causes low production of the active form of vitamin D, so Ca++ absorption in the small intestine is decreased.
  • Hypoparathyroidism is characterized by severe hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, resulting in tetany, carpopedal spasms, muscle and abdominal cramps, and tingling of the lips and hands. A positive Chvostek sign (tapping the face in front of the ear elicits tetany) and Trousseau sign (abnormal muscular contractions elicited by applying a blood pressure cuff) will often be noted.
  • Since the blood calcium levels are often very low, either calcium gluconate or vitamin D preparations should be administered to correct the condition. Vitamin D preparations, such as Cholecalciferol, elevate calcium levels, and also increase phosphate levels. Another treatment option would be to use the vitamin D3 analog calcitriol. Calcitriol has a mechanism of action similar to that of cholecalciferol. Ergocalciferol is also used, but has shorter duration and lower potency than cholecalciferol. Although further elevation of serum phosphate would be undesirable, vitamin D analogues are front-line therapy for hypoparathyroidism; phosphate levels may be addressed with phosphate binders or other measures.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 258

question_text: Which of the following is FALSE for deriphyline?
explanation:
• The methylxanthines have positive chronotropic and inotropic effects.
  • At low concentrations, these effects appear to result from inhibition of presynaptic adenosine receptors in sympathetic nerves increasing catecholamine release at nerve endings.
  • The higher concentrations (> 10 μmol/L, 2 mg/L) associated with inhibition of phosphodiesterase and increases in cAMP may result in increased influx of calcium.
  • At much higher concentrations (> 100 μmol/L), sequestration of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum is impaired.

Calcitrol has a mechanism of action similar to that of cholecalciferol. Ergocalciferol is also used, but has shorter duration and lower potency than cholecalciferol. Although further elevation of serum phosphate would be undesirable, vitamin D analogues are front-line therapy for hypoparathyroidism; phosphate levels may be addressed with phosphate binders or other measures.

question_text: A 56-year-old male is presented with lethargy and confusion. Labs were ordered, revealing serum calcium of 17 mg/dL. To rapidly lower his serum calcium, you administer calcitonin. However, calcitonin alone is insufficient because it is known to rapidly and suddenly lose its effectiveness within 2 to 3 days of repeated dosing. For this reason, a bisphosphonate, which take 2 to 3 days to become effective, is added simultaneously. What is the term for the rapid decrease in response to calcitonin?
explanation:
Tachyphylaxis describes a scenario in which the response to a drug rapidly decreases. Tachyphylaxis resembles tolerance in that the response to the drug cannot be restored by increasing the dose. There are some important differences between tolerance and tachyphylaxis, however. Tolerance is a slow decrease in response to a drug, whereas tachyphylaxis is rapid. Tolerance comes from the target cells or tissue modifying its physiology to compensate for the effect of a drug. Tachyphylaxis occurs when something disrupts the drug itself from functioning, such as internalization of receptors or uncoupling of signal transduction.

A. Anaphylaxis is a manifestation of a type I hypersensitivity reaction mediated by mast cells and preformed It does not lead to a decreased response in a drug’s action.

B. Prophylaxis refers to measures taken to prevent disease rather than treat disease once it occurs. It does not describe changes in response to a drug.

D. Tolerance and tachyphylaxis both refer to a decreased response to a drug, but tolerance has a slower onset and relates to changes in physiology to compensate for the drug’s effect.

question_text: A  2-year-old boy has passed 4-6 stools daily over the last 2 days. The faces are liquid and contain no blood or mucus. While awaiting medical evaluation, which of the following oral fluids is mosteffective to prevent dehydration in this patient?
option_c: Filtered water with no added solutes
explanation:
• Humans consume approximately 2 L of fluid each day and secrete an additional 7 L of fluid from upper digestive organs (eg, salivary glands, stomach, pancreas, gallbladder). Nearly all of this fluid is reabsorbed from the gastrointestinal lumen by the small intestine epithelium. The osmotic gradient for water reabsorption is largely established by the active cotransport of sodium into the apical end of enterocytes coupled with chloride, glucose, or amino acids. Sodium is then transported out of the basolateral end of the enterocyte (sodium/potassium ATPase), which pulls water down its osmotic gradient from the gastrointestinal lumen through the tight junctions between enterocytes and into the lamina propria (and ultimately the bloodstream).
  • This young patient who recently began going to day care likely has acute infectious diarrhea of a viral etiology (eg, rotavirus, norovirus). Infections that target the small intestine cause watery diarrhea by blocking the active transport of sodium chloride into the enterocyte or by increasing chloride excretion into the gastrointestinal lumen (mediated by elevated intracellular cyclic AMP, cyclic GMP, or calcium). In this setting, oral rehydration with a hypotonic, equimolar sodium-glucose solution maximizes water and sodium reabsorption by the remaining functional enterocytes, and is the most effective oral therapy for maintaining volume and electrolyte status in children with acute infectious diarrhea.

question_text: A 21-year-old woman comes to you for advice for contraception. Her menses are painful and occur at regular 30-day intervals with heavy flow. Moreover, DMPA is administered at 3-month intervals instead of daily, which facilitates patient adherence. Finally, DMPA is a good alternative for women with contraindications to estrogen therapy (e.g., migraine). Common side effects include breakthrough bleeding, a reversible reduction in bone mineral density, and a delay in return of fertility of up to 18 months after discontinuation.

question_text: A 68-year-old man comes to the office due to thigh and leg pain that worsens with exertion. The patient smokes 2 packs of cigarettes a day Which of the following drugs would best provide symptomatic improvement due to direct dilation of arteries and inhibition of platelet aggregation?
explanation:
• Several molecules, including thrombin, adenosine diphosphate, and thromboxane A2, activate platelets by acting on cell surface receptors. However, interference with post-receptor signaling can alter platelet function. In particular, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) activates a family of enzymes known as the cAMP-dependent protein kinases, or protein kinase A, and leads to inhibition of platelet aggregation. Agents that increase intra-platelet cAMP levels decrease platelet aggregation by preventing platelet shape change and granule release.
    • Cilostazol reduces platelet activation by inhibiting platelet phosphodiesterase, the enzyme responsible for the breakdown of cAMP. It is also a direct arterial vasodilator. The net effect is a decrease in claudication symptoms and an increase in pain-free walking distances in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD). Patients with PAD should be initiated on a graded exercise program, which has also been shown to improve symptoms.

question_text: A 30-year-old man undergoes surgery for a mitral valve replacement. Five days later, he develops non-blanching, darkened and purpuric lesions on his trunk and arms. Laboratory studies show WBC is 11,000/ ml, Hb is 14 mg/dL, and platelets are 70,000/ml. Administration of which of the following drugs is most appropriate for this patient?
explanation:
• This patient was most likely given heparin. The complication described here is known as heparin induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
  • It is caused by an IgG autoantibody that reacts with platelet factor 4 (PF4) on the platelet surface and forms an irreversible complex with heparin, which activates platelets leading to thrombosis and thrombocytopenia.
  • Obviously, in these cases, heparin should be stopped immediately. The patient should be switched to a direct thrombin inhibitor, such as bivalirudin, argatroban or the selective factor Xa inhibitor, fondaparinux.

There are two types of HIT.

  • Type 1 is a nonimmune response to heparin and begins 1-2 days after heparin initiation and occurs in 30% of heparin The resulting thrombocytopenia is mild to moderate; and the platelet count rarely falls below 100,000/ml.
  • Type 2 is immune-mediated and commonly known as heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and thrombosis (HITT). It is an uncommon but potential complication in patients receiving heparin intraoperatively. ITT is characterized by thrombocytopenia, thrombosis, and thromboembolic complications, including skin necrosis and gangrene. It typically occurs 4-14 days after initiation of heparin administration.

question_text: A 68-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of shortness of breath and tachycardia. A spiral CT scan of the chest shows a pulmonary embolism. Treatment with a medication that causes an almost immediate inactivation of factor lla is begun. Which of the following laboratory studies will most likely be used to monitor the effect of the drug administered to this patient?

• Heparin, an anticoagulant that accelerates the activity of antithrombin Ill (ATIll), thereby inactivating thrombin (factor Ila). More specifically, heparin binds reversibly to ATIll and causes an almost instantaneous inactivation of factors lla and Xa.
  • The heparin-ATIll complex can also inactivate factors IX, XI, XIl and plasmin. Heparin prevents progression of existing clots by inhibiting further clotting and the lysis of existing clots relies on endogenous thrombolytics.
  • Heparin is often administered to individuals diagnosed with acute embolism or thrombosis by continuous IV infusion at a rate sufficient to raise the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) to 5-2 times the control value.
  • The aPT measures the intrinsic system and common pathway, which is affected by factors I (fibrinogen), I (prothrombin), V, VIN, IX, X, XI, and XII.
  • In other words, the anticoagulant effect of heparin should be continually monitored to ensure that the patient's aPTT does not 5 to 2 times the control value.

question_text: A 65-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation is started on a new medication to prevent stroke. A few days later, she develops the painful, progressively necrotic skin lesion shown in the images (Image A: Day 4, Image B: Day 6). This is a classic example of which of the following drug's paradoxical adverse effects?
explanation:
• The images display classic features of Warfarin-induced skin necrosis, a rare but severe complication. Image A shows a sharply demarcated, erythematous, and purpuric lesion, which has progressed to a large, irregular, hemorrhagic, and necrotic bulla by Image B.

This is a paradoxical prothrombotic event.

  • Warfarin inhibits the synthesis of Vitamin K-dependent procoagulant factors (II, VII, IX, X) and anticoagulant proteins (Protein C and Protein S).
  • Protein C has a much shorter half-life than most of the clotting factors.
  • Therefore, after starting warfarin, there is a transient period where Protein C levels drop rapidly before the procoagulant factors are depleted. In a patient with an underlying Protein C deficiency, this creates a temporary but severe hypercoagulable state, leading to microthrombosis and skin necrosis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Clopidogrel (Option A): This is an antiplatelet agent. While bleeding is a side effect, it does not cause this type of thrombotic skin necrosis.

Enoxaparin (Option B): This is a Low-Molecular-Weight Heparin. It acts by potentiating antithrombin and does not cause a hypercoagulable state.

Heparin (Option C): The classic prothrombotic complication of heparin is Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT). While HIT can cause skin lesions at injection sites, the widespread, demarcated necrosis seen here is the pathognomonic presentation of warfarin necrosis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Warfarin-induced skin necrosis is a rare but classic adverse effect, typically occurring 3-10 days after initiating therapy.
  • The cause is a transient hypercoagulable state from the rapid drop in Protein C levels.
  • It is strongly associated with an underlying deficiency of Protein C or Protein S.

Reference:

Katzung BG. Basic & Clinical Pharmacology. 14th ed. McGraw-Hill; 2018: Page Number: 595.

question_text: 72-year-old man with a history of mitral valve replacement is currently taking an oral anticoagulant and also has his prothrombin time monitored on a regular basis. It also prevents thrombus formation in a variety of other situations, such as prosthetic valves. Warfarin increases prothrombin time (PT) and international normalized ratio (INR) because it interferes with the synthesis of the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors of the liver (II, VI, IX, and X) and therefore necessitates regular monitoring of the PT. Here is a summary to differentiate PT from aPTT:
  • The prothrombin time (PT), which is affected by warfarin, measures factors I (fibrinogen), Il (prothrombin), V, VII, and X. The PT is a measure of the extrinsic pathway of coagulation. The activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), which is affected by the heparins, measures the intrinsic pathway and common pathway

• Warfarin, a coumarin anticoagulant, inhibits epoxide reductase, which blocks the ability to activate vitamin K.
  • This prevents the vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of coagulation factors Il, VI, IX, and X, thus inhibiting their synthesis.
  • Warfarin similarly inhibits the vitamin-dependent synthesis of protein C and S, which have anticoagulant properties resulting from their inhibition of activated factors VIll and V.
  • Because warfarin acts by inhibiting the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors, the factors affected first will be those with the shortest half-lives, which are protein C and factor VIla.
  • Thus, warfarin has an initial paradoxical procoagulant effect because of a rapid reduction in protein C, while activity of most of the endogenous clotting factors (vitamin-dependent factors within the common and intrinsic coagulation pathways, I, IX, and X) persists.
  • This can lead to a state of hyper-coagulability and throm Warfarin may cause necrosis of the skin (typically on the breasts, buttocks, thighs, and abdomen) generally during the first several days of therapy.
  • The lesions are initially sharply demarcated, erythematous, and purpuric. They may resolve, or progress to large, irregular, hemorrhagic bullae that can eventually become necrotic.
  • Patients receiving a large loading dose of warfarin or who have an existing protein C deficiency are most susceptible. Warfarin should be discontinued immediately, and heparin, vitamin K, and protein C have been used in therapy. Despite treatment, approximately 50% of patients will require skin grafting.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number 834-33.

question_text: Identify the incorrect pair of drugs with their predominant action GPCR pathway.

let's explain each option:

  1. Mirabegron - Gi:

    • It predominantly acts through the Gi (inhibitory) protein pathway, leading to relaxation of the detrusor smooth muscle in the bladder.
    • This option is incorrect because the predominant GPCR pathway for Mirabegron is Gi, not Gq.

question_text: A 66-year-old man presents with complaint that he sees dark shadows that keep following him. He has a 6-year history of Parkinson disease treated with levodopa, carbidopa, and entacapone. The patient is admitted to the hospital and the dose of her antiparkinson medications is reduced. Four days later, the patient still feels threatened by the dark shadows that follow him. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
• Patients with PD are at an increased risk of developing psychosis (most commonly in the form of visual hallucinations) as a side effect of dopamine replacement therapy.
  • If other causes of psychotic symptoms have been excluded (e.g., infections) and adjusting the dose of antiparkinson medication does not provide symptomatic relief, as seen here, antipsychotic medication is indicated.
  • Quetiapine, or other second-generation antipsychotics like clozapine or pimavanserin, is the first-line option for patients with PD with persistent psychotic symptoms.
  • Patients taking quetiapine, especially elderly individuals, should be monitored for common side effects of drug, including anticholinergic stimulation, metabolic symptoms, and QT prolongation.
  • Options A and B- Haloperidol & Risperidone should not be used in patients with PD because it is a dopamine antagonist and has anticholinergic activity; it can exacerbate both motor and psychotic symptoms.
  • Option D- Benztropine is used in individuals with PD to manage tremor and rigidity. This patient, however, presents with signs of psychosis, which can worsen with the use of an anticholinergic drug.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 504-505

question_text: A 28-year-old woman is brought because of profound nausea, vomiting, headache, sweating, tachycardia, blurred vision, and dizziness. explanation:
• Helicobacter pylori (HP) is an acid-labile, spiral-shaped, gram-negative rod that is catalase-positive, oxidase-positive, and urease-positive. It resides in the mucosal layer and surface epithelial cells in the stomach. There is a strong association between HP and peptic ulcer disease (PUD). It is also associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and some lymphomas. Because this organism is difficult to eradicate with a single agent, a multiple medication regimen is often used.
  • Treatment regimens includes combinations of metronidazole, bismuth subsalicylate, omeprazole, and tetracycline or amoxicillin. This patient's signs and symptoms are highly suggestive of a disulfiram-like reaction caused by metronidazole. This reaction is caused by drugs that inhibit acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (similar to disulfiram) leading to an accumulation of acetaldehyde. Metronidazole, taken with alcohol, leads to elevated levels of acetaldehyde, which can cause headache, nausea and vomiting, facial flushing, tachycardia, sweating, blurred vision, dizziness, low blood pressure, and confusion.

question_text: A 26-year-old man comes to ED because of a 1-week history of worsening fatigue, nausea, and vomiting. Patient is on ATT.  Physical examination shows right upper quadrant tenderness and scleral icterus. Laboratory studies show elevated aminotransferases. Impaired function of which of the following pharmacokinetic processes is the most likely explanation for this patient's symptoms?
explanation:
Most metabolic biotransformations occur at some point between absorption of the drug into the circulation and its renal elimination. In general, all of these reactions can be assigned to one of two major categories called phase I and phase II reactions.

Phase I reactions usually convert the parent drug to a more polar metabolite. If phase I metabolites are sufficiently polar, they may be readily excreted. However, many phase I products are not eliminated rapidly and undergo a subsequent reaction in which an endogenous substrate such as glucuronic acid, sulfuric acid, acetic acid, or an amino acid combines with the newly incorporated functional group to form a highly polar conjugate.

question_text: A 72 years old woman complaints that sometimes she sees a dog in her kitchen and at other times she sees a snake in her garden, both of which no one else can see. A subcutaneous injection is used to "rescue"the patient that provides temporary relief. With which of the following drug you will pretreat to prevent nausea?
