question_text: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of the sudden onset of severe left eye pain, blurred vision, nausea, and vomiting. She has been taking phenylephrine to control URI symptoms.  Gonioscopy shows that the iris meets the cornea at an angle of 10° (N = 20-45°). Systemic pharmacotherapy is initiated with a drug. Which of the following additional adverse effects is most likely to occur in this patient?
explanation:
The patient's sudden-onset eye pain and blurred vision along with narrow iridocorneal angle confirms the diagnosis of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma. The patient received treatment with systemic acetazolamide.

Option A: Ocular allergy is known side effect of Alpha 1 agonist & Alpha 2 agonists.

Option B: Diaphoresis can be an adverse effect of parasympathomimetic drugs, including the topical ophthalmic formulations (e.g., pilocarpine) given in the treatment of acute primary angle-closure glaucoma. This patient, however, is receiving systemic treatment.

Option C: Bronchoconstriction can caused by systemic absorption of non selective topical beta-blockers like timolol.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 168.

question_text: A 72-year-old man is brought to the hospital due to severe chest pain and shortness of breath for the last several hours. Physical examination reveals bilateral crackles and a third heart sound. ECG shows ST elevation in multiple leads. He is started on infusion as shown below. Which of the following is most likely to be increased due to the medication used in this patient?
explanation:
Dobutamine is a beta adrenergic agonist with predominant activity on beta-1 receptors. (B1 > B2, Inotropic effects > chronotropic effects) It is used for management of refractory heart failure associated with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction and cardiogenic shock.

Effects of Positive inotropy and chronotropy: Increased cardiac contractility (potent effect) and heart rate (weaker effect), leading to increased cardiac output (improves end-organ perfusion) and decreased left ventricular filling pressures (improves pulmonary congestion/edema)

The strong inotropic effect of dobutamine significantly increases myocardial oxygen consumption, which can trigger or exacerbate myocardial ischemia. As such, dobutamine should not be used routinely in patients with decompensated heart failure. However, in patients with cardiogenic shock, this drawback is often outweighed by improvement in cardiac output and end-organ perfusion.

Option A: Dobutamine is a weak chronotropic agent that causes an increase in heart rate. This leads to a decrease in cardiac diastolic filling time

Option C: In the vasculature, the beta-2 agonist effects (vasodilation) of dobutamine are somewhat stronger than its alpha-1 agonist activity (vasoconstriction), resulting in overall mild vasodilation.

Option D: Dobutamine causes decreased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and left and right ventricular filling pressures due to the increased cardiac contractility.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 148.

question_text: A 54-year-old Mr. Green, had a cardiac transplant 6 months ago. His current blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg and heart rate is 100 bpm. Which of the following drugs would have the least effect on Mr Green's heart rate?
explanation:
Given clinical scenario in the patient of recent heart transplantation, involves cutting of the autonomic nerves to the heart. As a result, autonomic nerve endings degenerate, and cardiac transmitter stores are absent for 2 years or longer after surgery. Phenylephrine usually causes reflex bradycardia, which requires intact vagal innervation.

Note that denervation may result in up-regulation of both β1 and β2 receptors so that direct-acting β agonists may have a greater than normal effect like Nor-epinephrine and Isoproterenol (Option B & C)

Indirect-acting sympathomimetics are ineffective in changing heart rate due to degeneration of autonomic nerve ending. (Option A)

Reference: Basic & clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 15th Edition, pg no. 154

question_text: Action of drugs 'X' and 'Y' on heart rate with/without pre-treatment shown below in table. Find out drug X and Y respectively.
explanation:
Drug X causes slowing of the heart rate, but this is converted into tachycardia by hexamethonium and atropine, demonstrating that when it occurs, the bradycardia is caused by reflex vagal discharge. Phenoxybenzamine also reverses the bradycardia to tachycardia, suggesting that α receptors are needed to induce the reflex bradycardia and that also has direct β-agonist actions. So drug X = Norepinephrine

Drug Y causes tachycardia that is not significantly influenced by any of the blockers; therefore, drug Y must have a direct β-agonist effect on the heart. So drug Y = Isoproterenol.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 130.

question_text: A 72-year-old man presents with severe substernal chest pain and shortness of breath. Physical examination reveals bilateral crackles and a third heart sound. ECG shows ST elevation in multiple leads. The patient is diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction. He is started on dobutamine infusion and prepared for coronary catheterization. Which of the following is most likely to be increased due to the medication used in this patient?
explanation:
• Dobutamine is a beta adrenergic agonist with predominant activity on beta-1 receptors, weaker activity on beta-2 receptors, and minimal activity on alpha-1 receptors. It is used for management of refractory heart failure associated with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction and cardiogenic shock. Stimulation of beta adrenergic receptors results in increased production of cAMP in target cells and causes the following effects.
    • Positive inotropy and chronotropy: Increased cardiac contractility (potent effect) and heart rate (weaker effect), leading to increased cardiac output (improves end-organ perfusion) and decreased left ventricular filling pressures (improves pulmonary congestion/edema)
    • Mild vasodilation: Decreased systemic vascular resistance that often causes a slight reduction in blood pressure; this avoids the increase in afterload seen with other vasopressor/inotropic agents (eg, norepinephrine) but limits its usefulness in severely hypotensive patients
    • The strong inotropic effect of dobutamine significantly increases myocardial oxygen consumption, which can trigger or exacerbate myocardial ischemia. As such, dobutamine should not be used routinely in patients with decompensated heart failure. However, in patients with cardiogenic shock, this drawback is often outweighed by improvement in cardiac output and end-organ perfusion.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 193

question_text: A 67-year-old man presents with severe substernal chest pain and shortness of breath since 3 hours. Physical examination reveals bilateral crackles and a third heart sound. ECG shows ST elevation in multiple leads. The patient is diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction complicated by acute severe heart failure. He is started on dobutamine infusion and prepared for coronary catheterization. Which of the following is most likely to be increased due to the medication used in this patient?
explanation:
Dobutamine is a beta adrenergic agonist with activity on beta-1 receptors >> beta-2 receptors >> alpha-1 receptors. As such, dobutamine should not be used routinely in patients with decompensated heart failure. It is used for management of refractory heart failure associated with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction and cardiogenic shock. Stimulation of beta adrenergic receptors results in increased production of cAMP in target cells and causes the following effects:

  • Positive inotropy and chronotropy: Increased cardiac contractility (potent effect) and heart rate (weaker effect), leading to increased cardiac output and decreased left ventricular filling pressures. It increases myocardial oxygen consumption, which can trigger or exacerbate myocardial ischemia. However, in patients with cardiogenic shock, this drawback is often outweighed by improvement in cardiac output and end-organ perfusion.
  • Mild vasodilation: Decreased systemic vascular resistance that often causes a slight reduction in blood pressure; this avoids the increase in afterload seen with other vasopressor/inotropic agents (eg, norepinephrine) but limits its usefulness in severely hypotensive patients

A. Dobutamine is a weak chronotropic agent that causes an increase in heart rate. This leads to a decrease in cardiac diastolic filling time.

C. In the vasculature, the beta-2 agonist effects (vasodilation) of dobutamine are somewhat stronger than its alpha-1 agonist activity (vasoconstriction), resulting in overall mild vasodilation. The net hemodynamic effects are a decrease in systemic vascular resistance with or without a slight reduction in blood pressure.

D. Dobutamine causes decreased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and left and right ventricular filling pressures due to the increased cardiac contractility and output.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 216

question_text: After administering an intravenous injection of noradrenaline, there is a decrease in heart rate. What is the reason?
explanation:
Explanation:

Activation of α1-adrenergic receptors leads to contraction of vascular smooth muscle, resulting in vasoconstriction.

  • This increases systolic blood pressure, which depends on cardiac output and total peripheral resistance (TPR).
  • It also increases diastolic blood pressure, which is primarily dependent on TPR.

The rise in mean arterial pressure activates the baroreceptor reflex, which triggers a compensatory decrease in heart rate (reflex bradycardia).

Explanation of other options:

Stimulation of alpha 1 receptors (Option B): Alpha-1 receptors are responsible for vasoconstriction, but their activation does not directly cause a decrease in heart rate. The decrease in heart rate is due to the baroreceptor reflex triggered by the increase in blood pressure from alpha-1 receptor activation.

Activation of beta 1 receptors (Option C): Beta-1 receptors are responsible for increasing heart rate and contractility, and they are not the cause of the decrease in heart rate observed here. In fact, beta-1 activation would typically lead to an increase in heart rate, not a decrease.

Inhibition of baroreceptors (Option D): The baroreceptors are not inhibited by noradrenaline; instead, they are activated when blood pressure rises. The reflex mechanism works to reduce heart rate in response to increased blood pressure, not due to inhibition of the baroreceptors.

Key Takeaways:

Noradrenaline causes rise in systolic, diastolic and mean BP; it does not cause vasodilatation (no β2 action), peripheral resistance increases consistently due to α action.

question_text: A 72-year-old male presents with a weak urinary stream and frequent urination in small amounts. He is currently taking prazosin. He also reports frequent episodes of light-headedness and low blood pressure. Which of the following alpha-blockers would be a more suitable alternative for him?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient is showing signs of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and is experiencing postural hypotension, likely as a side effect of prazosin, a non-selective alpha-1 antagonist that acts on both vascular and urogenital alpha-1 receptors.

Tamsulosin, a selective alpha-1A receptor blocker, specifically targets receptors in the prostate and bladder neck. This improves urinary symptoms while having minimal impact on blood pressure, thereby reducing the risk of postural hypotension.

Explanation for other options:

Alfuzosin (Option A), Terazosin (Option B), and Doxazosin (Option D) primarily block alpha-1B receptors, leading to relaxation of both arterial and venous smooth muscle. This results in decreased peripheral vascular resistance and a reduction in blood pressure. However, they do not significantly improve urinary outflow and therefore are not ideal choices for treating BPH.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman with septic shock has persistent hypotension. Her blood cultures were positive for E. coli. Current medications include norepinephrine, ceftriaxone, and acetaminophen. Repeat blood cultures are negative. Her temperature is 99.5 F, heart rate 96/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Laboratory studies are shown. Which of the following is next line of management ?
option_d: Add glucocorticoids in current treatment regimen
explanation:
• This patient has persistent hypotension from her bacterial infection. Her labs indicate that she is slowly improving, and her low T3 is likely unrelated to her hypotension.
  • Sick euthyroid syndrome refers to abnormal thyroid hormone levels in critically ill patients who actually have intact thyroid function. A commonly seen pattern is low T3, with low-normal levels of T4 and TSH, as seen in this patient. While the exact underlying mechanism is not completely understood, increases in type 3 deiodinase and decreases in type 1 deiodinase occur; the net result is a decrease in T3 levels with normal T4 levels. Since the activity of type 2 deiodinase within the pituitary gland remains unaffected, conversion of T4 to T3 can occur within the pituitary gland. Therefore, stimulation of pituitary thyrotrophic cells often does not occur and TSH levels remain normal. Treatment of underlying illness is recommended. Thyroid hormone replacement is usually not recommended because thyroid function is normal (there is not conclusive evidence that thyroid hormone substitution is beneficial to patients with ESS)

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 690

question_text: A 56-year-old woman is presented with tachycardia, shortness of breath, and chest pain. She had had shortness of breath and diarrhea for the last 2 days and was sweating and anxious. TSH <0.01 mIU/L (normal 0.4-4.0 mIU/L). The diagnosis of thyroid storm was made. Which of the following is a drug that is a useful adjuvant in the treatment of thyroid storm?
explanation:
• In thyroid storm, β blockers such as propranolol are useful in controlling the tachycardia and other cardiac abnormalities, and propranolol also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.

Symptomatic treatment:

  • Hyperadrenergic symptoms: beta blockers are first-line
    • Preferred: Propranolol, due to combined beta-blockade and antithyroid effects
      • Pre-existing heart failure: esmolol
      • Mild obstructive airway disease/stable asthma: atenolol or metoprolol
    • Beta blocker contraindications: consider CCBs, e.g., diltiazem
  • Hyperthermia
    • External cooling techniques (e.g., ice packs, cooling blankets, alcohol washes)
    • Antipyretics, e.g., acetaminophen (Consider IV administration )
    • Avoid aspirin.
  • Hypotension and hypovolemia: fluid resuscitation to treat insensible and GI losses
    • Fluids containing 5–10% dextrose are preferred to meet the high metabolic demand.
    • Fluid requirement is often high (3–5 L/day).
  • Agitation: benzodiazepines, e.g., lorazepam

Antithyroid drugs in thyroid storm

  • Inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis
    • First line: propylthiouracil
    • Alternative: methimazole
  • Inhibition of thyroid hormone release (through the Wolff-Chaikoff effect)
    • First line: iodine solutions given at least 1 hour after antithyroid drugs
      • Potassium iodide solution
      • Lugol solution
    • In patients with iodine allergy or iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis, lithium can be used .
  • Inhibition of peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
    • Propranolol
    • Glucocorticoids: can also treat concurrent adrenal insufficiency
      • First line: hydrocortisone
      • Alternative: dexamethasone

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 702

question_text: An 85-year-old man develops bilateral pedal cyanosis and beginning necrosis of the toes 5 days after admission to the ICU for CAP and severe hypotension. The patient has received empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and vasopressors. All extremities are cold to touch. Which of the following intracellular changes is most likely to occur in vascular smooth muscle as a result of this drug?
option_a: Decreased activity of myosin light-chain kinase
option_b: Increased activity of protein kinase C
option_d: Increased activity of protein kinase A
explanation:
Given clinical scenario of bilateral necrosis of the toes and coldness of all extremities with history of CAP suggest a septic shock. The persistent vasoplegia associated with septic shock frequently requires prolonged treatment with vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial blood pressure > 65 mm Hg.

Norepinephrine is a vasopressor that preferentially agonises alpha-1 receptors, causing vasoconstriction and an increase in systemic vascular resistance. Prolonged alpha receptor agonism can cause distal arterioles and their branches (especially cutaneous branches) to constrict to the point of causing distal ischemia and consequent necrosis. This phenomenon is most commonly observed in the fingertips and distal toes and manifests with symmetrical discoloration and coldness.

Alpha-1 agonists (e.g., phenylephrine, norepinephrine, midodrine) are used to treat hypotension because increased protein kinase C activity through Gq GPCR patheway -> increases the concentration of intracellular calcium in vascular smooth muscle, which increases vascular smooth muscle contraction.

Option D : Protein kinase A (PKA) is involved in the Gs and Gi GPCR pathways. Activation of Gs protein ultimately leads to activation of protein kinase A. However, NE through alpha-1 receptors acts by Gq GPCR pathway.

Option A : Decreased myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK) activity in vascular smooth muscle would cause vasodilation, a deleterious effect in this patient with a septic shock. MLCK activity in muscle tissue is decreased by 3 mechanisms:

  • Closing L-type voltage-gated calcium channels through membrane repolarisation;
  • Decreasing intracellular calcium concentration through inhibtion of a Gq protein-receptor coupled receptor (While NE acts through alpha-1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle which increases intracellular calcium); and
  • Increasing the activity of protein kinase A through stimulation of Gs protein-coupled receptors.

Option C : Guanylate cyclase activity is increased in vascular smooth muscle by stimulation of ANP or BNP receptors and by drugs that increase nitric oxide concentration (nitrate drugs). Increased guanylate cyclase activity increases cGMP synthesis, which in turn activates myosin-light-chain phosphatase and causes smooth muscle relaxation. Nitroprusside is used to treat hypertensive crisis via this mechanism.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 146.

question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with complains of urinary retention. He has hypertension but not compliant with treatment. BP : 160/100. On DRE : an enlarged prostate rubbery consistency is felt. Which of the following drugs would be the most appropriate initial therapy ?
explanation:
This patient's urinary symptoms along with the prostatic findings on physical examination suggest benign prostatic hyperplasia. His blood pressure measurement is also diagnostic for hypertension. An α blocker is appropriate therapy in a man with both hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia because both conditions involve contraction of smooth muscle containing α receptors.

Terazosin is an α-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist, used to treat hypertension (↓ vasoconstriction →↓ blood pressure) as well (relaxation of bladder neck muscles →↓ bladder outlet obstruction and easier micturition). This patient with hypertension and symptoms of BPH would likely benefit from treatment with terazosin. Other medications that could also be used include prazosin and doxazosin.

Option A: Phenoxybenzamine is a sympatholytic drug commonly used pre-operatively in the management of pheochromocytoma. Because surgical manipulation of pheochromocytoma can release significant amounts of sympathetic hormones, nonspecific blockade of both α-1 receptors and α-2 receptors is necessary to prevent dangerous spikes in blood pressure intraoperatively and postoperatively. Phenoxybenzamine is not indicated for routine treatment of hypertension or to manage benign prostatic hyperplasia.

Option B: Tamsulosin is commonly administered in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia. Though tamsulosin is an antagonist on adrenergic receptors, its effect is selective for prostatic α-1A adrenergic receptors and α-1D adrenergic receptors. Tamsulosin has only a marginal effect on vascular α-1B adrenergic receptors and would not be the optimal treatment for this patient's hypertension.

Option D: Finasteride is a 5-α-reductase inhibitor that blocks the hyper-plastic growth of the prostate by inhibiting androgen synthesis. Though finasteride would be beneficial in the management of this patient's benign prostatic hyperplasia, it would not treat his hypertension.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 166.

question_text: Which of the following drugs promotes the movement of potassium back into cells?
explanation:
Explanation:

Epinephrine activates β₂-adrenergic receptors, which stimulate the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump.

  • This pump increases cellular uptake of potassium in exchange for sodium, leading to a shift of potassium from the extracellular fluid (plasma) into the intracellular compartment.
  • This mechanism is clinically relevant in the acute management of hyperkalaemia.

Explanation for other options:

Acetazolamide (Option B): A carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in the proximal tubule to increase bicarbonate excretion, producing mild diuresis. It does not influence transcellular potassium movement.

Atropine (Option C): A muscarinic receptor antagonist that reduces parasympathetic activity, but it has no role in altering potassium distribution between compartments.

Lactic acid (Option D): Formed during anaerobic glycolysis; contributes to metabolic acidosis but does not directly facilitate intracellular potassium uptake.

question_text: Which of the following drugs act through intracellular receptors?
explanation:
Thyroid hormones act through intracellular receptors which activate a nuclear transcription factor.

  • Intracellular receptors (Nuclear receptor superfamily) are slowest acting.
  • These may be present in the cytoplasm
    • Glucocorticoids
    • Mineralocorticoids
    • Vitamin D
    • Androgen
  • In the Nucleus
    • Thyroid hormones (T3, T4)
    • Retinoic acid
    • PPAR
  • Both types of receptors finally act by nuclear mechanisms (i.e. by affecting transcription).
  • All the intracellular receptors are considered a part of 'Nuclear Receptor Superfamily'.

Options B,C,D: Glucagon, Epinephrine and Parathormone tend to bind to transmembrane receptors.

question_text: An elderly male presents with tremors and rigidity, and examination reveals a mask-like facial expression. Which of the following medications would be appropriate for his management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The elderly patient shows features consistent with Parkinson's disease, characterized by tremors, rigidity, slowness of movement (bradykinesia), and a reduced facial expression known as "masked facies" for which selegiline can be used.

  • In Parkinson's disease, degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra causes reduced dopamine in the striatum, leading to motor problems like rigidity and tremors.
  • Selegiline, an MAO-B inhibitor, works by blocking dopamine breakdown in the brain, thereby raising its levels and improving motor control.
  • It is frequently given in combination with levodopa/carbidopa as part of therapy.
  • This drug is particularly valuable in the early phase of Parkinson's disease when levodopa/carbidopa by itself is insufficient to manage symptoms.

Explanations of other options:

Clozapine (Option A): Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic mainly prescribed for schizophrenia and other severe mental illnesses, blocks dopamine receptors and may aggravate the symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Donepezil (Option B): Donepezil, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in Alzheimer's disease, works by boosting acetylcholine levels in the brain but does not improve the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Haloperidol (Option D): Haloperidol, a typical antipsychotic used in the management of schizophrenia and acute psychosis, acts by blocking dopamine receptors but may exacerbate Parkinsonian symptoms due to its dopamine-blocking effects.

question_text: A 54-year-old man is presented with an acute onset of severe ocular pain and blurred vision that is associated with halos around lights. The painful episode began when he walked into a dark room. Ophthalmologic examination shows erythema of the left eye. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate for this patient?
explanation:
• The patient is clearly presenting with signs and symptoms of acute angle-closure glaucoma. Primary acute angle-closure glaucoma occurs because of closure of a pre-existing narrow anterior chamber angle, as is commonly found in the elderly, hyperopes, and Asians. Symptoms can be triggered when a patient's pupils dilate, for example when entering a dark room, or if he or she takes a drug with anticholinergic side effects, such as scopolamine or tropicamide. Patients often seek immediate medical attention because of the intense pain and blurred vision. The blurred vision is characteristically associated with halos around lights. The eye is often very red and steamy, and the pupil is dilated and nonreactive to light; tonometry reveals elevated intraocular pressure.
  • Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, is a first-line agent that should be used systemically immediately. It reduces bicarbonate production in the ciliary epithelium, thus decreasing aqueous humor production. Mannitol is another agent used systemically to decrease IOP. It is a hyperosmotic agent that causes a fluid shift from the eye into the vascular space. Topical timolol (beta-blocker), apraclonidine (alpha-2 agonist), and pilocarpine (muscarinic agonist) are also used to aid in decreasing IOP. Patients are maintained on medication until a more definitive laser peripheral iridotomy can be performed.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 259

question_text: A 26-year-old man with chest discomfort occurs with climbing stairs. Family history includes an uncle who died suddenly at the age of 35 years. Apical impulse is strong and sustained. He has a soft crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the apex and left sternal border while supine that becomes quite pronounced when he stands up. Which of the following medications should be avoided while treating this patient's condition?
explanation:
• This patient's presentation, family history of premature sudden death, and systolic murmur that accentuates with standing from a supine position is consistent with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients with HM have dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction that worsens with decreased left ventricular (LV) volume (as can be caused by decreased preload and/or reduced systemic vascular resistance). As such, medications that generally should be avoided in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy include:
    • Vasodilators (eg, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, nitroglycerin, and ACE inhibitors) decrease systemic vascular resistance, leading to decreased afterload and lower LV volumes.
    • Diuretics decrease LV venous filling (preload) and also result in greater outflow obstruction.
  • In contrast, negative inotropic agents such as beta blockers (metoprolol), nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil), and disopyramide reduce LVOT obstruction and are helpful in symptomatic patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In addition, beta blockers may also help reduce anginal symptoms by decreasing myocardial oxygen demand.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 206

question_text: Which of the following beta-blockers is effective in patients with reduced ejection fraction and has been shown to reduce mortality in chronic heart failure without causing long-term worsening of the condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bisoprolol is a cardioselective beta blocker that is beneficial in chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). It helps improve heart function, reduce symptoms, and reduce mortality over time in heart failure patients.

  • Beta-blockers that have been proven to improve the survival of patients with HFrEF/Chronic HF are
    • Bisoprolol
    • Metoprolol
    • Carvedilol

Explanation for other options:

Propranolol (Option A) is a non-selective beta blocker, which blocks both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors. It is not typically preferred in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction as it may cause bronchospasm due to beta-2 receptor blockade and has less favourable long-term outcomes compared to cardioselective beta blockers like bisoprolol.

Pindolol (Option C) is a non-selective beta blocker with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA), meaning it partially stimulates beta receptors while blocking them. This property is generally not ideal in chronic heart failure, as it may not provide the same mortality benefits as other beta-blockers without ISA.

Esmolol (Option D) is a short-acting, cardioselective beta blocker typically used for acute conditions like arrhythmias and perioperative hypertension. It is not used for long-term management of chronic heart failure.

Learning Outcome:

The following 4 beta blockers are clinically tested and approved for the treatment of heart failure:

question_text: A 34 years old female patient came to OPD with the complaints of cough and mild difficulty in breathing at night times since 2 months. She gave history that difficulty in breathing happens particularly in cold atmosphere. On examination, bilateral wheezing was heard over the lung fields. Her Chest X Ray showed increased lung field area both side with tubular heart. She was diagnosed as bronchial Asthma. Physician start combination therapy of inhalational beta agonist and corticosteroids. Beta agonist causes bronchodilation by ____________.
explanation:
• The adrenoceptor agonists have several pharmacologic actions that are important in the treatment of asthma. They relax airway smooth muscle and inhibit release of bronchoconstriction mediators from mast cells.
  • They may also inhibit microvascular leakage and increase mucociliary transport by increasing ciliary activity.
  • As in other tissues, the β agonists stimulate adenylyl cyclase and increase the formation of intracellular cAMP.


Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 341

question_text: A 72-year-old woman with chemotherapy-related cardiomyopathy and now has an ejection fraction of 15%. She has been hospitalised two times in the last 6 months with acute decompensated heart failure. She is currently NYHA class IV regarding symptoms. What drugs can use continuously to support quality of life as a bridge therapy while waiting for transplantation ?
explanation:
As per clinical scenario, patient is in stage D of CHF. Orthotopic heart transplantation is the gold standard therapy for patient. Milrinone or dobutamine therapy (inotropic support) can be used continuously to support quality of life as a palliative goal or as a bridge to initiation of mechanical support or transplantation. However, studies show that the use of inotropes negatively impacts survival.

A,B & D : These drugs are used in CHF stage A,B and C. Not in D. Beta blocker may negatively impact cardiac output. While spironolactone and ACEIs can be used but it may decrease mortality till patient is in stage C of CHF.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 224

question_text: A patient was on metoprolol therapy for hypertension. He was also administered verapamil. Which of the following is likely to happen with above combination therapy?
explanation:
• Beta blockers like metoprolol depress the heart. They decrease the heart rate, conduction as well as contractility
  • Calcium channel blockers like verapamil and diltiazem also depress the heart.
  • Beta blockers should never be combined with verapamil or diltiazem due to additive cardiac depression leading to severe bradycardia and AV block.

question_text: A 68-year-old man is on metoprolol, ACEIs and Chlorthalidone for his cardiac condition. Which of the following drug should be avoided to prevent AV block  ?
explanation:
As given, in patient on metoprolol, should be avoided concurrent use of verapamil as, may cause AV blockade, sinus node depression and also heart failure.

Causes of AV block include Electrolyte disorders: e.g., hyperkalemia, Cardiotoxic drugs: e.g., beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, or digoxin (therapeutic doses or overdoses) and Other toxicity: e.g., carbon monoxide, cyanide.

Adapt management depending on the suspected underlying cause Discontinue or reduce medications causing AV block in case of Beta blocker toxicity, Digoxin toxicity or CCB toxicity.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 224

question_text: A 60-year-old man with COPD comes to the you with palpitations and dizziness since 1 week. Her pulse is 75/min and regular, BP is 3.110/80 mm-Hg. An ECG is shown. What is the first line therapy for her ?
explanation:
This patient's symptoms and ECG findings (narrow QRS complexes with an atrial rate of 240/min in a sawtooth pattern) are most consistent with atrial flutter. A mainstay of treatment of stable atrial flutter is to normalize the ventricular heart rate (rate control). However Consider rhythm control in the following patient groups:

  • Failure of rate control strategy to control symptoms or achieve target heart rate (80bpm)
  • New-onset Atrial flutter
  • Acute illness that precipitated Atrial flutter
  • Other: tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, pregnancy, patient preference, younger patients

Drugs used for rate control include beta-blockers (e.g., esmolol, propranolol, metoprolol) and non-DHP CCBs (e.g., diltiazem, verapamil). Verapamil is commonly used as first-line therapy as rate control for atrial flutter particularly in patient with COPD, as beta blockers are to avoided in them. (Option B)

Option C : Flecainide, Selective use and state-dependent block of Na; slowed conduction velocity and pacemaker activity primarily used for Refractory ventricular arrhythmias. It can increased arrhythmias and CNS toxicity.

Option D : Amiodarone, strong K block produces marked prolongation of action potential and refractory period. Group 1 activity slows conduction velocity, group 2 and 4 activity confer additional anti-arrhythmic activity, used only for Refractory arrhythmias. Some of the side effects include thyroid abnormalities, deposits in skin and cornea, pulmonary fibrosis, optic neuritis, torsades (rare).

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 245

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the pharmacological relationship between imipramine and diphenhydramine?
explanation:
Explanation:

Imipramine (a tricyclic antidepressant) blocks muscarinic (M) receptors as a notable adverse effect (anticholinergic): dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia. It is also a potent inhibitor of norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake (primary antidepressant action).
Diphenhydramine (a first-generation H1 antihistamine) also has significant antimuscarinic activity - this causes its characteristic sedation and anticholinergic side effects.

Therefore, the shared pharmacologic action between these two drugs is muscarinic receptor blockade

Diphenhydramine is not a NE-reuptake inhibitor, and neither drug "inhibits the other's action" pharmacologically in the way the stem suggests. (Options A, B, D Ruled Out)

question_text: Which antidepressant among the following exerts its therapeutic effect by blocking the reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine, thereby enhancing synaptic concentrations of these neurotransmitters?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Venlafaxine is a Serotonin-Norepinephrine Reuptake Inhibitor (SNRI).
  • Mechanism of Action:
    • Inhibits reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) → improves mood and reduces anxiety.
    • Inhibits reuptake of norepinephrine (NE) → increases alertness and energy, also contributing to antidepressant effect.
  • Clinical Uses: Major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, neuropathic pain.

Explanation of Other Options

Fluoxetine (Option A):

  • Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
  • Only inhibits serotonin reuptake, minimal effect on norepinephrine.

Paroxetine (Option C):

  • SSRI
  • Primarily blocks serotonin reuptake; used for depression, anxiety, and OCD.

Dapoxetine (Option D):

  • SSRI
  • Short-acting, used for premature ejaculation, not standard depression therapy.

explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Venlafaxine o Important SNRIs are :- Venalafaxine, Milnacipram, desvenalafaxine, Duloxetine.

question_text: A 44-year-old man comes to you with abdominal ultrasound shows an atrophic, hyper-echoic, nodular liver. An upper endoscopy is performed and shows dilated submucosal veins 2 mm in diameter with red spots on their surface in the distal oesophagus.  Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's oesophageal findings?
explanation:
This scenario suggest patient with cirrhosis with esophageal varices. Apart from the management of cirrhosis, primary prophylaxis against a variceal bleed should be initiated to prevent a haemorrhage that could be fatal.

Nonselective beta blockers like nadolol and propranolol are the primary prophylactic agent of choice against a variceal bleed in patients with small (< 5 mm in diameter), nonbleeding varices, as seen here. Nonselective beta blockers cause splanchnic vasoconstriction, decreasing portal blood flow and portal pressure, thereby reducing both the enlargement of varices and the risk of hemorrhage.

Beta-blocker treatment in patients suffering from advanced liver cirrhosis (Child class C) may lead to circulatory dysregulation. In these cases, the use of esophageal band ligation is the best alternative. Beta blockers should not be used in acute variceal bleeds as they decrease blood pressure and blunt physiologic elevation of HR.

Option B: Nitrates are a class of vasodilatory drugs that have been shown to reduce portal pressure. However, nitrates have not been shown to decrease bleeding rates and are therefore not recommended as a primary prophylaxis against variceal bleeding.

Option C: Metoprolol is a selective beta-1 antagonist that primarily acts on the beta receptors in the heart and is therefore ineffective in the management of esophageal varices.

Option D: Intravenous octreotide is used in the management of acute esophageal variceal bleeding as it rapidly reduces portal pressure and helps achieve hemostasis, thus enabling endoscopic therapy of a bleeding varices. However, due to tachyphylaxis, it is not suitable as a prophylactic agent against variceal bleeding.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 166.

question_text: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician for intermittent episodes of sharp chest pain and palpitations. She appears nervous. Her pulse is 115/min and irregularly irregular, and blood pressure is 139/86 mmHg. Examination shows a fine tremor on both hands and digital swelling; the extremities are warm. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
The condition underlying this patient's arrhythmia causes a state of adrenergic hyperactivity due to hyperthyroidism.

Propranolol is indicated for the immediate control of symptoms in patients with hyperthyroidism. Thyroid hormones affect cardiac myocytes directly and also stimulate proliferation of beta-adrenergic receptors, which can cause cardiac arrhythmias as seen in this patient. Beta blockers decrease the adrenergic tone and therefore improve tachycardia, hypertension, muscle weakness, tremor, and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Propranolol, in high doses, also decreases the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 by inhibiting the 5', monodeiodinase enzyme.

Option A : Warfarin is an oral anticoagulant. Patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) are at increased risk of developing thromboembolic complications, which is why long-term anticoagulation is indicated when the CHA2DS2-VASc score is ≥ 2 or when AF is caused by valvular disease. Although this patient has features of AF (irregularly irregular pulse), her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 1 and she has no history of valvular disease.

Option C : Propylthiouracil (PTU) is an antithyroid drug that is used in the medical treatment for hyperthyroidism, of which this patient shows sign and symptoms. However, symptomatic treatment should be started for immediate control of symptoms.

Option D : Amiodarone is used in the treatment of ventricular tachycardia and persisting ventricular fibrillation (VF) after unsuccessful defibrillation, as well as the long-term treatment of refractory supraventricular arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation). Because of the high levels of iodine in amiodarone, it may aggravate pre-existing thyroid conditions.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 168.

question_text:
A 68-year-old woman presents with lethargy and confusion. She is oriented only to person. Her temperature is 94.6OF, Pulse rate 49/min, respirations are 9/min, and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. The pupils are 7 mm and reactive to light. Deep tendon reflexes are 1+ bilaterally. Physical examination shows ,periorbital edema non pitting edema in both lower extremities and healed needle track marks in both antecubital fossae. Serum studies show a sodium concentration is 131mEq/L, a potassium concentration of 4.9 mEq/L, and a glucose concentration is 54mg/dl. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shown below. An ECG shows bradycardia, low voltage QRS complex, widespread T-wave inversion. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

1. Naloxone
2. Sodium bicarbonate
3. Hydrocortisone
4. Liothyronine
5. Levothyroxine
6. Epinephrine
7. IV fluids
explanation:
• Altered mental status in combination with hypothermia, bradypnea (causing respiratory acidosis with hypoxemia due to hypoventilation), hypotension, bradycardia, and features of myxedema heart disease (low-voltage QRS complexes, flattened or inverted T waves) and non-printing edema is suggestive of myxedema coma. Hyponatremia and hypoglycemia can be due to myxedema coma itself or a concomitant adrenal
  • Treatment with liothyronine and levothyroxine should be started immediately upon clinical suspicion of myxedema coma because this condition can be life-threatening (up to 50% mortality); patients should also be treated with glucocorticoids until a diagnosis of coexisting adrenal insufficiency is ruled out. This patient probably had a longstanding undiagnosed or untreated hypothyroidism, which increases the risk of developing myxedema coma. Moreover, her presumed history of injection drug use (healed needle track marks) is an additional precipitating factor for this condition. Other triggers include infections, stroke, acute coronary syndrome, trauma, and surgical procedures. In patients with suspected myxedema coma, blood samples for evaluation of TSH, T4, and cortisol levels should be drawn before initiating treatment. The treatment must then be initiated without waiting for the results.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 693

question_text: Initial Drug of choice for suspected case of acute adrenal insufficiency is:
explanation: Answer is C (Dexamethasone): The treatment of choice for acute adrenal insufficiency is Glucocorticoid Replacement Therapy. In cases where the diagnosis of acute adrenal insufficiency is suspected (not confirmed) Dexamethasone is preferred as the initial steroid of choice because Dexamethasone does not compete with the cortisol assay. Cosyntropin stimulation testing may be performed while the patient is on treatment.

question_text: Additional treatment with inhalational beta agonists is needed when FEV1 is less than ____ % of predicted.
explanation:
• Bronchodilators, such as inhaled albuterol, are rapidly effective, safe, and inexpensive.
  • Patients with only occasional symptoms of asthma require no more than an inhaled β 2 -receptor agonist take on an as-needed basis.
  • If symptoms require this “rescue” therapy more than twice a week, if nocturnal symptoms occur more than twice a month, or if the FEV 1 is less than 80% predicted, additional treatment is needed.
  • The treatment first recommended is a low dose of an inhaled corticosteroid, although treatment with a leukotriene receptor antagonist or with cromolyn may be used.
  • Theophylline is now largely reserved for patients in whom symptoms remain poorly controlled despite the combination of regular treatment with an inhaled anti-inflammatory agent and as-needed use of a β 2 agonist.

Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 351

question_text: A 65 years old male patient came to emergency department with complaint of severe dyspnoea. He refuses to lie down. His SpO2 on air is 75%, Respiration Rate (RR) is 24/min, pulse rate is 124/min, BP is 130/86 mm Hg. Oxygen therapy started immediately. On examination bilateral crepitus was heard over lung fields and Chest X Ray showed Emphysematous changes. On asking, relatives of the pt. gave history of chronic smoking. He was diagnosed as COPD. Which beta agonist should be administered for management of acute attack of dyspnoea?
explanation:
• In the management COPD, Short acting beta agonists are preferred for acute attacks of dyspnoea.
  • Salmeterol and Indacaterol are long acting beta agonist agents and used mainly as prophylaxis.
  • For relief of acute symptoms, inhalation of a short-acting β agonist (e.g., albuterol), of an anticholinergic drug (e.g., ipratropium bromide), or of the two in combination is usually effective.
  • For patients with persistent symptoms of exertional dyspnea and limitation of activities, regular use of a long acting bronchodilator, whether a long-acting β agonist (e.g., Salmeterol) or a long-acting anticholinergic (e.g., tiotropium) is indicated.
  • For patients with severe airflow obstruction or with a history of prior exacerbations, regular use of an inhaled corticosteroid reduces the frequency of future exacerbations.

Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 353

question_text: A 43-year-old woman is admitted with difficulty breathing. Examination reveals significant laryngeal edema. Which of the following drugs is the most effective physiologic antagonist of mediator responsible in smooth muscle?

B. Loratadine is a pharmacologic antagonist of histamine at these receptors.

C. Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist used to prevent postsurgical and chemotherapy-induced vomiting.

D. Ranitidine is a pharmacologic histamine antagonist that blocks the H2 receptor in the stomach and the heart, not H1 receptors in smooth muscle. The answer is A.

question_text: A patient with glaucoma presents to the emergency department with an acute asthma attack. Which antiglaucoma medication is the most probable cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Timolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that inhibits both β1 and β2 adrenergic receptors. Blockade of β2-receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle can lead to unopposed constriction, potentially triggering bronchospasm and acute asthma attacks, especially in susceptible individuals.

Explanation of other options:

Betaxolol (Option B): A relatively cardioselective β1-blocker with less affinity for bronchial β2-receptors, making it less likely to cause bronchospasm.

Latanoprost and Bimatoprost (Option C and D ): These are prostaglandin analogs that work by increasing uveoscleral outflow. They have no activity on beta-adrenergic receptors and do not cause bronchospasm.

Key Takeaways:

  • Non-selective beta-blockers are contraindicated in patients with asthma or COPD.
  • Cardioselective beta-blockers or prostaglandin analogs are safer choices for glaucoma patients with reactive airway disease.

question_text: Which of the following drugs is not used in the treatment of bronchial asthma?
explanation:
Explanation:

question_text:
Identify drugs acting on shown by ARROW in given illustrated image.

1. Betaxolol
2. Brimonidine
3. Bimatoprost
4. Brinzolamide
5. Dipiverfine
6. Physostigmine
7. Pilocarpine
explanation:
The arrow in the image points at inner non-pigmented ciliary epithelium (NPE) cells. These cells are responsible for production and secretion of Aqueous humor. Drugs acting on this site are responsible for decreasing the secretion of Aqueous humor.

  • Glaucoma is a major cause of blindness, primarily due to increased intraocular pressure (IOP).
  • It often responds to drug therapy, especially in the chronic form.
  • Primary manifestation: Increased IOP without initial symptoms.
  • Untreated glaucoma leads to retinal and optic nerve damage, visual field restriction, and blindness.
  • Two major types: open-angle and closed-angle (narrow-angle) glaucoma.
  • Closed-angle glaucoma is associated with a shallow anterior chamber and requires emergency treatment or surgical intervention.
  • Open-angle glaucoma is a chronic condition treated primarily with medications.
  • Strategies for open-angle glaucoma treatment: Reduce aqueous humor secretion and enhance aqueous outflow.

Drug Groups for Glaucoma Treatment

  • Cholinomimetics:
    • Examples: Pilocarpine, Carbachol, Echothiophate, Dorzolamide
  • α Agonists:
    • Examples: Brimonidine, Apraclonidine, Clonidine, Epinephrine
  • β Blockers:
    • Examples: Timolol, Betaxolol, Levobunolol, Carteolol
  • Prostaglandin F2α Analogs:
    • Examples: Latanoprost, Bimatoprost, Travoprost, Tafluprost
  • Diuretics:
    • Examples: Acetazolamide, Methazolamide, Dorzolamide (also a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor)

Also the set of drugs can be classified according to two different classification which depend upon the

  • Decreased synthesis of aqueous humor and
  • Increased aqueous humor flow

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung, Pg no. 167.

question_text: Which of the following can be prescribed for a patient with open angle glaucoma with bronchial asthma?

Though ocular irritation and pain are relatively frequent, no systemic side effects are reported. Blurring of vision, increased iris pigmentation, thickening and darkening of eyelashes have occurred in some cases. Macular edema can develop during treatment with any PGF2α analogue, especially in aphakic patients; a watch should be kept to detect it early.

Because of good efficacy, once daily application and absence of systemic complications, PG analogues have become the first choice drugs for open angle glaucoma. High cost is a disadvantage.

question_text: A 70-year-old man with chronic myopia comes to the ophthalmologist for regular check-up. Examination shows bilateral narrowing of peripheral visual fields, cupping of the optic discs, and elevated intraocular pressure. Gonioscopy shows no abnormalities. Which of the following first line of treatment for this patient ?
explanation:
The loss of peripheral vision, optic disc cupping, and elevated intraocular pressure in this patient with a normal gonioscopy are diagnostic of open-angle glaucoma.

Preferred first-line therapy are topical prostaglandin analogs like Latanoprost. Alternative options are Topical beta blockers alone and/or alpha-2 agonists OR Topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. For treatment of Refractory glaucoma, oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are used.

question_text: A chronic alcoholic patient with alcoholic liver disease was treated with anti-amoebic drugs. Subsequently, the patient developed symptoms including nausea, vomiting, flushing, and low blood pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient’s symptoms of nausea, vomiting, flushing, and hypotension after taking an anti-amoebic drug, along with a history of chronic alcohol use, suggest a disulfiram-like reaction.

Metronidazole, commonly used to treat amoebic colitis and liver abscesses, can cause this reaction due to its structural similarity to disulfiram, a medication used to support alcohol dependence treatment.

Disulfiram works by irreversibly inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH), and metronidazole produces a similar effect on ALDH. This inhibition leads to the buildup of acetaldehyde when alcohol is consumed, causing the characteristic symptoms.

Explanation for other options:

Delirium tremens (Option A): is a severe form of alcohol withdrawal that usually develops 48-72 hours after the last drink in chronic alcohol users. It is characterized by confusion, hallucinations, extreme agitation, and autonomic instability, and can also cause cardiac arrhythmias.

Alcohol withdrawal (Option B): occurs when a chronic alcoholic abruptly stops drinking. Symptoms typically include tremors, anxiety, insomnia, nausea, sweating, and sometimes seizures. However, the combination of flushing and hypotension after drug intake is more indicative of a disulfiram-like reaction in this scenario.

Hallucinosis (Option D): involves visual or auditory hallucinations during acute intoxication or alcohol withdrawal in alcoholics. The symptoms described in this patient align more closely with a drug-alcohol interaction reaction rather than hallucinations.

Learning Objective:

Drugs causing disulfiram-like reaction: (Mnemonic- CGMP)

(These are contraindicated in active alcoholics)

  • Chlorpropamide
  • Cephalosporins (mnemonic- PMTX):
    • CefoPerazone
    • CefaMandole
    • CefoTetan
    • CefoXitin
  • Griseofulvin
  • Metronidazole
  • Procarbazine

question_text:
Adverse effects of depolarizing agents are...
1. Hyperkalemia
2. Hypokalemia
3. Increased intraocular pressure
4. Decreased intraocular pressure
5. Increased intragastric pressure
6. Muscle pain
explanation:
• Hyperkalemia
    • Patients with burns, nerve damage or neuromuscular disease, closed head injury, and other trauma can respond to succinylcholine by releasing potassium into the blood, which, on rare occasions, results in cardiac arrest.
  • Increased Intraocular Pressure
    • Administration of succinylcholine may be associated with the rapid onset of an increase in intraocular pressure (< 60 seconds), peaking at 2–4 minutes, and declining after 5 minutes. The mechanism may involve tonic contraction of myofibrils or transient dilation of ocular choroidal blood vessels. Despite the increase in intraocular pressure, the use of succinylcholine for ophthalmologic operations is not contraindicated unless the anterior chamber is open (“open globe”) due to trauma.
  • Increased Intragastric Pressure
    • In heavily muscled patients, the fasciculations associated with succinylcholine may cause an increase in intragastric pressure ranging from 5 to 40 cm H 2 O, increasing the risk for regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents. This complication is more likely to occur in patients with delayed gastric emptying (eg, those with diabetes), traumatic injury (eg, an emergency case), eesophage dysfunction, and morbid obesity.
  • Muscle Pain
    • Myalgias are a common postoperative complaint of heavily muscled patients and those who receive large doses (> 1.5 mg/kg) of succinylcholine.

Reference :

LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 27- Skeletal muscle relaxants by Dr. Marieke Kruidering-Hall,PhD,& Dr. Lundy Campbell,MD. Page no. 474

question_text: A 20-year-old woman is taking diphenhydramine for severe hay fever. Which of the following adverse effects is she most likely to report?
explanation:
Diphenhydramine, older first generation H1 blocker, are highly sedating agents with significant autonomic receptor-blocking effects. These drugs should not be consumed before operating machinery. A newer subgroup of first-generation agents is less sedating and has much less autonomic effect. Chlorpheniramine and cyclizine may be considered prototypes.

The second-generation H1 blockers, typified by cetirizine, fexofenadine, and loratadine, are far less lipid soluble than the first-generation agents and have greatly reduced sedating and autonomic effects. All H1 blockers are active by the oral route.

H1 blockers do not activate muscarinic receptors, mediate vasoconstriction, or cause vertigo. Some relieve vertigo or motion sickness. They do not cause nervousness or anxiety. Diphenhydramine is a potent sedative with H1- and M3-blocking actions.

Overview of effects of antihistamine agents

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 283

question_text: The patient who suffered from arrhythmia was given Ivabradine that is a funny current blocker. Which of the following is not correct regarding funny currents (HCN channels).
option_d: Located in eyes and helps in vision
explanation:
Located in Heart (SA node):

  • Funny currents, or HCN channels, are indeed located in the heart, particularly in the sinoatrial (SA) node, contributing to pacemaker activity.

Helps in heart rate generation:

  • HCN channels play a vital role in generating the heart rate by allowing sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) ions to flow, which is essential for pacemaker activity.

Opened by Cyclic AMP:

  • This is incorrect; HCN channels are primarily activated by cyclic GMP, not cyclic AMP.

Located in eyes and helps in vision:

  • HCN channels are also present in the retina and are involved in visual processes, which supports the correctness of this statement.

Why Not Other Options

  • A: HCN channels are located in the heart, particularly in the SA node.
  • B: They are essential for heart rate generation by controlling the depolarization in pacemaker cells.
  • D: HCN channels are located in the eyes and contribute to visual signaling.

Key Takeaways:

HCN channels (funny currents) are crucial for heart rate regulation and visual processes. They are located in the heart and eyes, activated by cyclic GMP, making option C incorrect. Understanding their functions enhances knowledge of cardiac electrophysiology and vision.

question_text: A 69-year-old man comes with chest tightness when he walks uphill or climbs stairs. The patient is prescribed a medication that is metabolized to S-nitrosothiols in the vascular smooth muscle cells, and he reports rapid and significant symptom relief. Which of the following components of the cardiovascular system is most susceptible to the medication prescribed to this patient?
explanation:
• This patient has stable angina pectoris and experienced rapid symptomatic relief following receipt of a nitrate. Pharmacologic nitrates (eg, nitroglycerin, isosorbide mononitrate, isosorbide dinitrate) are metabolized to nitric oxide and S-nitrosothiols via mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase within vascular smooth muscle cells. These compounds in turn activate guanylate cyclase and promote the conversion of guanosine triphosphate to cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), which leads to dephosphorylation of myosin light chains and causes vascular smooth muscle relaxation.
  • Nitrates predominantly affect the large veins, where smooth muscle relaxation leads to venodilation and increased venous capacitance. Cardiac venous return (preload) is reduced, leading to a reduction in left ventricular end-diastolic volume and pressure and a consequent decrease in left ventricular wall stress. Decreased myocardial oxygen demand leads to relief of anginal symptoms.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 190

question_text: Which one of the following is not a nitric oxide donor but causes it to be synthesized and released from endogenous precursors, resulting in vasodilation?
explanation:
Nitroprusside and organic nitrites (eg, amyl nitrite) and nitrates (eg, nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate, and isosorbide mononitrate) contain NO groups that can be released as NO. Arginine is the normal source of endogenous NO. Acetylcho- line, acting on M3 receptors, stimulates the synthesis of NO from arginine.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung

question_text: A patient presents with sudden chest pain. After administering nitroglycerin sublingually, the pain subsides within a minute. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
explanation:
Explanation:

The chest pain relief following sublingual nitroglycerin is due to the release of nitric oxide, which leads to vasodilation of the coronary arteries. This dilation increases blood flow to the ischemic areas of the heart muscle, alleviating the pain.

Explanation for other options:

Release of endothelin (Option A): Release of endothelin from endothelial cells acts as a powerful vasoconstrictor, increasing vascular tone and blood pressure. It is not used in the treatment of angina.

Calcium channel blockade (Option C): It achieved by calcium channel blockers like amlodipine and verapamil, inhibits L-type calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle and cardiac cells, causing vasodilation, reduced heart rate, and decreased contractility. However, this mechanism is not how nitroglycerin treats angina.

Beta blockade (Option D): It involves beta-blockers such as atenolol and metoprolol, which block beta-adrenergic receptors, lowering heart rate, myocardial contractility, and oxygen demand. Nitroglycerin does not act on beta-adrenergic receptors.

question_text: A 75-year-old man with chronic stable angina is on sublingual nitroglycerin on SOS basis. While discussing a plan to start isosorbide dinitrate therapy, the patient becomes concerned about the high dose of oral isosorbide dinitrate compared to sublingual nitroglycerin. Which of the following is the most likely reason for using a high dose of oral nitrate?
explanation:
• Nitrates, beta blockers, and calcium channel blockers are the mainstay of therapy for patients with chronic stable angina. Sublingual nitroglycerin is the therapy of choice in acute episodes for immediate relief of angina and for prevention of angina prior to engaging in strenuous physical activity. Chronic nitrate therapy with long-acting oral formulations (isosorbide dinitrate or mononitrate) is used to prevent recurrent anginal episodes in patients with chronic stable angina.
  • Sublingual nitroglycerin is absorbed rapidly from oral mucosa directly into the venous circulation and has a rapid onset of action within 2-5 minutes. Long-acting isosorbide dinitrate is absorbed via the gastrointestinal tract and undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism in the liver prior to release in the systemic circulation. This leads to low bioavailability and the need for much higher doses of oral formulations as compared to sublingual nitroglycerin.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 218

question_text: A 60-year-old male is diagnosed with exertional angina. His treatment regimen includes metoprolol, isosorbide dinitrate and aspirin. He takes isosorbide dinitrate early in the morning and again in the afternoon, but he does not take an evening dose. Such a pattern of drug administration is intended to decrease which of the following?
explanation:
• Around-the-clock nitrate administration (in any form) rapidly results in development of tolerance to nitrates. This is why a nitrate-free interval must be provided every day in patients that are using daily long acting nitrates. The mechanism by which this occurs has not been fully demonstrated, but it is theorized that it is due to a decreased vascular sensitivity to nitrates and an increased sensitivity to endogenous vasoconstricting agents. Usually the nitrate-free period is timed to occur during the night when the patient is sleeping and cardiac work is the least.

question_text: A 28-year-old woman complains of fever, fatigue, weight loss, arthralgia, and transient patchy alopecia during the last 3 months. She is on treatment for a cardiovascular disease. Antinuclear antibody testing is positive. Presently, her hematocrit is 33% and creatinine is 1.2 mg/dL. The most likely cause ?
explanation:
Several drugs can cause a syndrome resembling systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). The syndrome is most common with procainamide, which induces the presence of antinuclear antibodies in up to 75% of individuals within a few months. There is a genetic predisposition to drug- induced lupus determined by drug acetylation rates.

  • Genetic susceptibility
    • Decreased acetyltransferase activity resulting in slow acetylation of drugs
    • Presence of HLA-DR2, HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, or an unexpressed C4 complement allele
  • Common drug triggers (SHyPS)
    • Sulfa drugs
    • Certain nonsulfa drugs, e.g., procainamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, methyldopa, minocycline, phenytoin, TNF-α inhibitors

Typical symptoms include systemic complaints and arthralgias. The initial therapeutic approach is withdrawal of the offending drug.

  1. Although ethosuximide has been reported to cause drug-induced SLE, case reports have been mainly anecdotal.
  2. Drug- induced lupus is exceedingly rare with the use of oral contraceptives.
  3. Phenytoin has not been shown in clinical studies to cause a lupus-like reaction.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 224

question_text: A 65-year-old man with known CAD comes with exertional chest tightness. The patient underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery 3 years ago for progressive angina. You discuss about adding isosorbide dinitrate to his current therapy but the patient is concerned about adverse effects. Which of the following is most likely to occur in this patient with the add-on therapy?
explanation:
• Nitrates are frequently used for symptomatic relief in patients with chronic stable angina. The anti-ischemic effect of nitrates is mediated by systemic vasodilation (predominantly venodilation) with a decrease in left ventricular end-diastolic volume and wall stress, resulting in decreased myocardial oxygen demand and relief of angina symptoms. The main adverse effects seen with nitrate therapy include headaches, cutaneous flushing, lightheadedness, hypotension, and reflex tachycardia. Nitrates must be avoided in patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (due to increased outflow tract obstruction), right ventricular infarction (due to reduction in preload, impairing cardiac output), and those on phosphodiesterase inhibitors (synergism increases the risk of severe hypotension).

question_text: Manufacturer of a drug company labels the drug as containing 500 mg paracetamol. On quantitative analysis by the authorities, it was found to contain only 200 mg of drug. According to drugs and cosmetics act 1940, this type of drug is known as?
explanation:
This is a misbranded drug.

Spurious Drugs

A drug shall be deemed to be spurious if

  • It is manufactured under a name which belongs to another drug or It is an imitation of another drug or
  • It has been substituted partly or wholly by another drug or
  • It wrongly claims to be a product of another manufacturer.
  • Contaminated and misbranded drugs.

Misbranded Drugs

A drug shall be deemed to be misbranded:

  • If it is so colored, coated, powdered or polished that damage is concealed or if it is made to appear of better or greater therapeutic value than it really is; or
  • If it is not labelled in the prescribed manner; or
  • If its label or container or anything accompanying the drug bears any statement, design or device which makes any false claim for the drug or which is false or misleading in any particulars.

Adulterated Drugs

For the purposes of this chapter, a drug shall be deemed to be adulterated:

  • If it consists in whole or in part, of any filthy, putrid or decomposed substance; or
  • If it has been prepared, packed or stored under insanitary conditions whereby it may have been contaminated with filth or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health; or
  • If its container is composed, in whole or in part, of any poisonous or deleterious substance which may render the contents injurious to health; or
  • If it bears or contains, for purposes of coloring only, a color other than one which is prescribed; or
  • If it contains any harmful or toxic substance which may render it injurious to health; or
  • If any substance has been mixed therewith so as to reduce its quality or strength.

Reference: Drugs and Cosmetics Act

question_text: A 43-year-old woman comes with occasional chest discomfort as a mid-line pressure or squeezing sensation that lasts 10 minutes and is accompanied by diaphoresis. The patient has no history of hypertension or diabetes mellitus but is an active smoker. Ambulatory ECG monitoring shows transient ST-segment elevations in leads I, aVL, and V1-V4 during an episode of chest pain at night. Which of the following would most likely provoke this patient's chest pain?
explanation:
Patient's Clinical Presentation:

  • Chest discomfort, diaphoresis, and transient ST-segment elevations during chest pain episodes at night.

Diagnosis Suggestion:

  • Highly suggestive of variant angina (Prinzmetal's angina).
  • Characterized by coronary artery vasospasms, leading to reduced blood flow to the heart muscle and chest pain.
  • Smoking is a significant risk factor for this condition.

Diagnostic Test:

  • To confirm Prinzmetal's angina, perform a coronary vasospasm provocation test.
  • Administer a vasospastic agent like Dihydroergotamine.

Reason for Using Dihydroergotamine (Correct Answer - Option B):

  • Dihydroergotamine can provoke chest pain in Prinzmetal's angina patients, aiding in diagnosis.
  • It induces coronary artery spasms, reproducing the patient's symptoms during a controlled test.

Explanation for Incorrect Options:

A) Amlodipine:

  • Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker used to prevent angina and improve blood flow.
  • Not suitable for diagnostic testing as it aims to prevent, not provoke, symptoms.

C) Morphine:

  • Morphine is an opioid analgesic used to relieve chest pain during acute angina episodes.
  • Not used for diagnostic purposes to provoke symptoms.

D) Phentolamine:

  • Phentolamine is an alpha-blocker with adrenergic receptor actions.
  • Not a standard agent for provoking coronary artery vasospasms or diagnosing Prinzmetal's angina.

In summary, Dihydroergotamine is chosen as the diagnostic tool because it induces coronary artery spasms, a characteristic feature of Prinzmetal's angina. The other options are either medications used for angina treatment or have different mechanisms unsuitable for this diagnostic purpose.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 216

question_text: Drugs used for treatment of advanced endometrial carcinoma?
explanation:
Pembrolizumab is a humanized monoclonal IgG4-κ isotype antibody that blocks interaction between PD-1 and its ligands. This humanized antibody has a mouse variable region grafted onto a human antibody framework and shows high affinity toward PD-1 receptors of humans and other primates but no appreciable affinity for mouse or rat PD-1.

The FDA has extended the approval for pembrolizumab to any cancer with mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H). The defects in DNA repair lead to a higher mutation load and increased generation of mutant protein antigen by cancer cells that can activate the immune system. This first cancer tissue-agnostic approval extends immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment to subsets of patients with hereditary CRC due to Lynch syndrome (MSI-H) and up to 20% of patients with sporadic colon cancer. The frequency is less in endometrial, ovarian and pancreatic cancers and will require testing of each patient's tumor to assess suitability of the treatment.

question_text: A 50-year-old male is given digitalis for the treatment of atrial fibrillation. Which is not correct regarding digitalis
option_a: Inhibits the Na+/K+ATPase pump of myocardial fibers
explanation:
Inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump:

  • Digitalis inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump in myocardial fibers, leading to increased intracellular calcium ([Ca²+]), which enhances cardiac contractility.

Increases vagal tone:

  • Digitalis increases vagal tone, helping to control the ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation, contrary to option B.

Decreases ventricular filling pressure:

  • It improves left ventricular emptying and subsequently decreases ventricular filling pressures, making it beneficial in heart failure.

Increases contractility:

  • Digitalis augments myocardial contractility, enhancing cardiac output and supporting heart function.

Why Not Other Options

  • A: Digitalis effectively inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
  • C: It reduces ventricular filling pressure due to improved emptying.
  • D: Digitalis enhances contractility, improving cardiac output.

Key Takeaways:

Digitalis is crucial in managing atrial fibrillation and heart failure by increasing contractility and vagal tone while inhibiting the Na+/K+ ATPase pump. It does not decrease vagal tone, making option B incorrect. Understanding these effects is essential for effective cardiac care.
