question_text: A 57-year-old woman with "fainting spell", her blood pressure is 120/60 when lying down and 60/20 when she sits up. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of her fainting spell?
explanation:
• The case history suggests that the syncope (fainting) is associated with diuretic use. Complications of diuretics that can result in syncope include both postural hypotension (which this patient exhibits) due to excessive reduction of blood volume and arrhythmias due to excessive potassium loss. Potassium wasting is more common with thiazides (because of their long duration of action), but these drugs rarely cause reduction of blood volume sufficient to result in orthostatic hypotension.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 262

question_text:
A 27-year-old girl with a history of major depression and bulimia is brought to the emergency department after a suicide attempt. She claims to have ingested several pills. She has also been very thirsty. Her temperature is 98°F, blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 14/min. Physical examination shows dry oral mucosa and reduced skin turgor.
Laboratory results are as follows:


Which of the following medications did this patient most likely ingest?
explanation:
• As per given clinical scenario, the patient has consumed diuretic which can cause hyponatremia, hypokalemia and hypercalcemia. Thiazide diuretics match the given description.
  • Loopdiuretics function by inhibiting the absorption of solutes within the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop, a process that is critical for maintenance of the corticomedullary concentration gradient. As a result, patients on loop diuretics are unable to maximally concentrate their urine and thus lose substantial amounts of both salt and water in the urine. In contrast, patients taking thiazides have a normal corticomedullary concentration gradient and are better able to retain free water in response to increased vasopressin levels. Thus, patients taking thiazide diuretics are more likely to retain free water and develop hyponatremia.
  • Thiazide diuretics can also lead to hypercalcemia secondary to increased proximal and distal tubule Ca++ reabsorption.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 264

question_text: Which of the following diuretics will most likely result in afferent arteriole vasoconstriction?
explanation:
• Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, thereby impairing HCO3- and Na+ absorption and causing an osmotic diuresis. One consequence of this diuresis is that the tubule fluid arriving at the macula densa is relatively NaCI-rich.
  • The macula densa is a specialized region of the loop of Henle's thick ascending limb (TAL) designed to sense tubule NaCI levels. Na+ and Cl- enter macula densa cells via the Na+-K+-2CC cotransporter (NKCC). CI then exits the cell via a basolateral CI channel causing depolarization and generating a sensory signal that travels within the juxtaglomerular apparatus to the glomerular arterioles.
  • The afferent arteriole (AA) constricts and the efferent arteriole (EA) dilates as a result, thereby reducing glomerular filtration pressure and glomerular filtration rate (GFR). With the filtered Na+ load now reduced, less NaCl is presented to the macula densa and signaling stops. This signaling pathway is known as tubuloglomerular feedback (TGF) and is designed to optimize GFR in the face of changing glomerular perfusion pressures. Acetazolamide thus mimics the effect of inappropriate increases in GFR in a healthy individual.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 256

question_text: A psychiatrist prescribes lithium for a patient diagnosed with bipolar disorder. Which of the following statements is not true regarding lithium?
option_a: Lithium is teratogenic if given to pregnant females
option_b: Lithium toxicity is exacerbated with thiazide
option_c: Lithium can decrease thyroid hormone levels
option_d: Hemodialysis is not useful in lithium overdose
explanation:
Explanation:

Hemodialysis is effective in managing lithium overdose, as it quickly clears lithium from the blood and is particularly useful in cases of severe toxicity, hence making Option D the right answer.

Explanations of other options:

Lithium toxicity is exacerbated with thiazide (Option B): Thiazide diuretics, like hydrochlorothiazide, reduce the kidney's clearance of lithium, which raises its blood levels and may cause toxicity, presenting with symptoms such as tremors, confusion, and kidney dysfunction.

Lithium can decrease thyroid hormone levels (Option C): Lithium can lower thyroid hormone levels by inhibiting their production and release, leading to hypothyroidism. Therefore, patients on lithium therapy require regular monitoring of thyroid function.

question_text:
Which of the following diuretics matches its primary site of action correctly?
1. Osmotic diuretics -Distal convoluted tubule
2. Thiazide diuretics - Proximal convoluted tubule
3. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors - Proximal convoluted tubule
4. Potassium-sparing diuretics - Collecting duct
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Osmotic diuretics primarily act in the proximal convoluted tubule and loop of Henle, not the distal convoluted tubule (Option A & D Ruled Out).
  • Thiazide diuretics act in the distal convoluted tubule, not the proximal convoluted tubule (Option A, C & D Ruled Out).
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., Acetazolamide) act in the proximal convoluted tubule.
  • Potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g., Spironolactone, Amiloride) primarily act in the collecting duct.

question_text: A patient sustains a head injury in a road traffic accident and shows signs of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). Which diuretic is the most suitable for reducing ICP in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic commonly used in clinical practice to reduce increased intracranial pressure (ICP). It works by drawing water out of the brain and into the bloodstream, thereby reducing cerebral oedema and lowering ICP.

question_text: A patient diagnosed with ascites due to cirrhosis. The diuretic of choice to reduce edema would be?
explanation:
Aldosterone antagonists like Spironolactone and Eplerenone are the drugs of choice for Cirrhotic edema, resistant edema and hypertension.

Uses of Spironolactone & Eplerenone

It is a weak diuretic in its own right and is used mostly in combination with other more efficacious diuretics.

  1. To counteract K+ loss due to thiazide and loop diuretics.
  2. Edema: Spironolactone is more useful in cirrhotic and nephritic edema in which aldosterone levels are generally high. It potentiates thiazides and loop diuretics and is frequently added to them in the treatment of ascites due to cirrhosis of the liver. It breaks resistance to the thiazide/loop diuretic that develops due to secondary hyperaldosteronism and re-establishes the response. Thus, spironolactone is particularly employed in refractory edema.
  3. Hypertension: Spironolactone is used to augment a thiazide in the treatment of resistant hypertension.

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Thiazide diuretics work mainly by blocking the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT) of the nephron.

Under normal conditions, this symporter reabsorbs sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-

By inhibiting this transporter, thiazides decrease the reabsorption of Na+-

This leads to diuresis, reducing blood volume, which helps lower blood pressure and relieve edema associated with conditions like congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, chronic renal failure, and acute glomerulonephritis.

Explanation for other options:

Blockade of the Na-Cl symporter (Option A): is actually the mechanism of loop diuretics like furosemide, which inhibit the Na-K-2Cl symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, not in the distal convoluted tubule.

Blockade of aldosterone receptors (Option C): describes how aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone work. These drugs block aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct and distal tubule, increasing sodium excretion while conserving potassium.

Blockade of epithelial sodium channels (Option D): refers to the action of potassium-sparing diuretics like amiloride, which block sodium channels in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption and preventing potassium loss.

Learning Objective:

question_text: For which of the following conditions are high-ceiling (loop) diuretics not a primary treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) are not a primary treatment for pulmonary hypertension. The mainstay of therapy targets vascular pathology and includes vasodilators like calcium channel blockers, endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE5 inhibitors, and prostacyclin analogs. Diuretics are only used adjunctively to manage right heart failure-associated fluid overload.

Loop diuretics inhibit the Na⁺-K⁺-2Cl⁻ symporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, promoting sodium, potassium, and chloride excretion. They are used to remove excess fluid in hepatic, renal, and cardiac diseases. Their combined diuretic and vasodilatory effects cause natriuresis, lower left ventricular filling pressures, and rapidly relieve pulmonary edema.

Explanation of other options:

Generalized edema : A primary indication for loop diuretics to reduce extracellular fluid volume. B) Cerebral edema: Loop diuretics like furosemide can be used, often with mannitol, to reduce intracranial pressure. C) Acute pulmonary edema: A classic indication where IV furosemide provides rapid preload reduction and diuresis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Loop diuretics treat fluid overload states but not the underlying vascular pathology of pulmonary hypertension.
  • Their mechanism involves inhibiting the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb.

question_text: A patient with hypertension and chronic kidney disease presents with recurrent episodes of renal colic. Which diuretic is most suitable for use in this clinical scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

A hypertensive patient with chronic kidney disease (CKD) experiencing frequent attacks of renal colic would benefit from Hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic.

  • It helps manage hypertension and can reduce calcium excretion in urine, which is beneficial for preventing calcium-based kidney stones, a common cause of renal colic.

Explanation for other options:

Furosemide (Option A) is a loop diuretic that indeed causes increased calcium excretion in the urine, which can exacerbate symptoms of renal colic.

Mannitol (Option B), an osmotic diuretic, is used in acute settings and is not suitable for chronic conditions like CKD and renal colic.

Spironolactone (Option D), a potassium-sparing diuretic, is typically used for heart failure or aldosterone excess but not for preventing kidney stones or controlling hypertension in CKD.

question_text: A 34 yr old male with hypertension diagnosed with stage 4 chronic kidney disease with eGFR<30 ml/min. His doctor wants to prescribe a thiazide diuretic. Which of the following can be given?
explanation:
Metolazone and Indapamide are two thiazide diuretics that can be administered even in patients with renal insufficiency.

Metolazone: In common with loop diuretics, it is able to evoke a clinically useful response even in severe renal failure (g.f.r. ~15 ml/min), and has marked additive action when combined with furosemide. An additional proximal tubular action has been demonstrated; PO4 reabsorption that occurs in PT, is inhibited. It is excreted unchanged in urine. Metolazone has been used mainly for edema.

question_text: A 65-year-old African American man comes to the you for a follow-up examination after presenting with elevated blood pressure readings during his last visit. His pulse is 70/min and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacotherapy for this patient?
explanation:
• This patient meets the diagnostic criteria for initiating treatment.

Indication for pharmacological therapy

  • BP ≥ 140/90 mm Hg
  • BP ≥ 130/80 mm Hg with a 10-year ASCVD risk of ≥ 10% (e.g., age ≥ 65 years, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, stable ischemic heart disease, peripheral artery disease, and/or previous stroke)
  • According to the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA), as well as the Eight Joint National Committee (JNC-8), chlorthalidone is a preferred first-line drug for African American patients with isolated hypertension.
    • Thiazide diuretics are considered especially effective antihypertensive agents because impaired salt excretion and subsequent intravascular volume expansion are thought to be the primary drivers of hypertension in this patient group. Hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and hypercalcemia are all adverse effects of chronic chlorthalidone use; hyperglycemia, especially, limits the use of chlorthalidone in patients with metabolic syndrome.
    • Amlodipine can also be used as a first-line therapy in African American patients, particularly those with metabolic syndrome.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 178

question_text: Side effect of thiazide diuretics are all except ?
explanation: Ans. is 'A' i.e., Hypocalcemia Thiazides cause hypercalcemia (see above explanation).

question_text: A 50-year-old woman was prescribed a diuretic by a doctor to manage hypertension. Which of the following diuretic acts on the site 'A' is marked in the given image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Site A represents the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), where Hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretic, works by blocking sodium and chloride reabsorption. This results in greater excretion of sodium, chloride, and water.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man comes with severe pain with tenderness in his first metatarsophalangeal joint. He says that the pain was so bad that it woke him up from sleep. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
Laboratory studies show WBC count is 12 x 103/mL , creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, calcium is 8.6 mg/dL, and uric acid is 9.5 mg/dL.
explanation:
• Acute gouty arthritis (AGA) is characterized by the rapid onset of pain, swelling, and inflammation.
  • The attack is often monoarticular at first, affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint.
  • Uric acid levels are generally >7.5 mg/dL when an attack occurs. Changes in rate levels, leading to gout flares, can result from acute alcohol intoxication, overindulgence of foods high in purines, rapid weight loss, dehydration, and trauma. Medications (e.g., thiazide or loop diuretics, allopurinol, uricosuric agents, Low-dose aspirin) can also precipitate gout.

Mnemonic : THe NIce PYRAmid

Thiazides(+loop diuretics), niacin, pyrazinamide, aspirin

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 262

question_text: What is the mechanism of renal calculi formation in a patient on Hydrochlorothiazide?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hydrochlorothiazide leads to decreased citrate excretion, which is linked to renal calculi formation.

  • Hypocitraturia refers to reduced citrate levels in the urine and represents a significant metabolic abnormality strongly linked to kidney stone formation.
  • Citrate normally binds to calcium, preventing it from forming crystals and stones.
  • Insufficient citrate increases calcium stone risk, making hypocitraturia one of the most common yet treatable causes of nephrolithiasis.

Etiology:

  • Citrate excretion depends on gastrointestinal alkali absorption. Low urinary citrate can result from high meat and sodium intake with poor fruit consumption, medications such as thiazides, ACE inhibitors, topiramate, and acetazolamide.
  • Conditions like IBS, chronic diarrhoea, short bowel syndrome, and post-bariatric surgery are also implicated.
  • Hormonal and metabolic factors also play a role: higher levels are seen in women, influenced by estrogens, vitamin D, and growth hormone, whereas testosterone, starvation, and acidosis reduce levels.

Citrate prevents stone formation by multiple mechanisms:

  1. Binding calcium to reduce crystal availability.
  2. Directly inhibiting crystal growth and aggregation.
  3. Raising urinary pH, improving uric acid solubility.
  4. Limiting osteopontin and other stone matrix components.
  5. Reducing the stone-promoting effect of urinary proteins like Tamm-Horsfall protein.
  6. Increasing urine viscosity, which reduces crystal aggregation.

Explanation of other options:

Increased calcium excretion (Option A): Thiazide diuretics lead to decreased calcium excretion.

Decreased calcium excretion (Option B): Decreased calcium excretion is seen with thiazide use, which is beneficial in patients with osteopenia and hypercalciuria.

Increased oxalate absorption (Option C): Thiazide diuretics have no measurable effect on urinary oxalate excretion.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK564392/

 https://www.auajournals.org/doi/10.1097/01.ju.0000076371.92938.9b#:~:text=Conclusions%3A,be%20detected%20in%20clinical%20practice.

question_text: A 45-year-old male is presented to the ED with severe tachycardia after a drug overdose. His family reports that he has been depressed. Past history of hypertension is present. Which one of the following drugs increases the heart rate in a dose-dependent manner?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The scenario describes the overdose of a drug in a hypertensive patient which causes tachycardia which points towards class of anti-hypertensive which causes increases heart rate.
  • Direct vasodilators (Option D) regularly increase heart rate (by reflex tachycardia), and Minoxidil, a very efficacious vasodilator, causes severe tachycardia that must be controlled with β blockers.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Option A & C : Captopril (ACE inhibitors) and Losartan (ARB), do not significantly increase heart rate as they're predominantly acts by inhibiting RAAS. Compensatory responses to blood pressure lowering by these drugs are minimal.
  • Option B : Hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide diuretics, acts by Inhibition of Na+-Cl- co-transporters in the early distal tubule segment leads to diuresis. It lower blood pressure by reduction of blood volume. Compensatory responses to blood pressure lowering by diuretics are minimal.

question_text: A 62-year-old man who is a chronic smoker with chronic congestive heart failure presents for follow-up. He is currently taking captopril and hydrochlorothiazide. Which of the following changes would be increased as a result of this therapy
explanation:
ACE inhibitors and thiazides may improve the clinical signs of heart failure. As such, patients may have some improvement in how they feel and may be able to ambulate without as much exertion.

ACE inhibitors decrease vascular resistance, venous tone, and blood pressure. These drugs reduce preload and afterload, resulting in an increased cardiac output. ACE inhibitors also blunt the usual angiotensin II–mediated increase in epinephrine and aldosterone seen in HF. ACE inhibitors improve clinical signs and symptoms in patients also receiving thiazide or loop diuretics and/or digoxin.

  • Vascular resistance will decrease in patients taking an ACE inhibitor.
  • Venous tone will decrease in patients taking an ACE inhibitor.
  • Jugular venous distension is a clinical sign that may improve with ACE inhibitor.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 219

question_text:
A 65-year-old man comes with shortness of breath on exertion. Physical examination shows bilateral 2+ pitting edema of the lower limbs, and faint crackles are heard on auscultation of the chest. Treatment is begun with a drug. A few days later, the man returns to the physician because of muscle weakness. Laboratory studies show:
Arterial PCO2 = 48 mm Hq
Arterial pH = 7.49
Plasma HCO3 = 35 mEq/L
Which of the following is most likely decreased in this patient?
explanation:
• The data indicate that the man has developed metabolic alkalosis (increased PCO2, pH, and HCOz),which occurs commonly with overuse of diuretics (thiazides and loop diuretics). The loop diuretics act by inhibiting the reabsorption of sodium, potassium, and chloride in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle by interfering with the chloride binding of the Na+/K+/2CI cotransport system, thus affecting electrolyte transfer in the distal tubule.
  • This cotransport system normally reabsorbs about 25% of the sodium load; thus, inhibition of this pump can cause a substantial increase in the distal tubular concentration of sodium, reduced hypertonicity of the surrounding interstitium, and less water reabsorption in the collecting duct.
  • Furthermore, diuretics that block sodium reabsorption at segments above the collecting ducts (loops and thiazides) will increase sodium load to the collecting tubules and ducts ("downstream"). This results in increased loss of potassium and subsequent loss of hydrogen ions resulting in alkalosis.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 263

question_text: A 39-year-old male presents with symptoms of stress and inability to manage work-life balance. On evaluation, his blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_d: Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has Stage 1 hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg). In adults <55 years, ACE inhibitors or ARBs are preferred as first-line therapy.

  • Telmisartanis an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB).
    • Provides 24-hour BP control.
    • Cardioprotective and renoprotective.
    • Metabolically neutral.
  • In patients with diabetes mellitus, ACE inhibitors or ARBsare strongly recommended because they reduce intraglomerular pressure, slow progression of diabetic nephropathy, and improve cardiovascular outcomes.

Lifestyle modification (diet, exercise, stress management) must always accompany drug therapy, but pharmacological treatment is indicated at this stage to prevent long-term complications.

Explanation of Other Options:

Start glucocorticoids (Option A): Glucocorticoids can induce or worsen hypertension by sodium and water retention.

Start thiazide (Option C): Thiazide diuretics are effective antihypertensives and part of first-line therapy, particularly in elderly patients and those with volume-dependent hypertension. However, in a younger patient (<55 years), guidelines recommend starting with an ACE inhibitor or ARB instead of a diuretic.

Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment (Option D): Lifestyle modification is crucial but not sufficient alone in this case. The patient already has Stage 1 hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) and requires pharmacological therapy to prevent long-term complications such as stroke, myocardial infarction, chronic kidney disease, and heart failure.

question_text: A 27-year-old woman presents with severe headache and vomiting during high-altitude hiking. Therapy is initiated with Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that alkalinizes the urine. What is the primary site of action of this drug in the nephron?
option_b: Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle
explanation:
• This patient has symptoms of altitude sickness. The pharmaceutical treatment of choice for altitude sickness is acetazolamide, a urine alkalinising agent.
  • Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide enhance bicarbonate elimination in the proximal convoluted tubule. Bicarbonate diuresis results in urine alkalinization as well as normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. The latter drives compensatory respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation) and thus speeds the acclimatization process of altitude sickness by increasing the blood oxygen concentration and reducing carbon dioxide levels.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 256

question_text: A patient presents with complaints of patches in the oral mucosa, as shown below, with a burning sensation on taking spicy food for the past 6 months. Which of the following drugs can cause this side effect?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario, along with an image showing lacy reticular lesions, is suggestive of lichenoid drug eruptions, which are seen with the use of beta-blockers.

  • Lichenoid reactions can be triggered by a wide range of medications, including antihypertensives such as ACE inhibitors, β-blockers, and calcium channel blockers.
  • Other drugs implicated are diuretics like furosemide, NSAIDs, aspirin, proton pump inhibitors, and statins.
  • Vaccinations, such as hepatitis B, and checkpoint inhibitors for cancer therapy are also recognised triggers.
  • These reactions may present as photodistributed eruptions (lichenoid photoeruptions) or as generalised lesions.
  • They can appear as plaques, sometimes with Wickham striae, papules, or exfoliative erythema. Photolichenoid reactions commonly affect extensor surfaces, including the backs of the hands.
  • Oral involvement is less common than in idiopathic lichen planus but can occur, especially with imatinib, appearing as plaques or erosions; the lower lip is frequently affected. Nails may also be involved and sometimes represent the only site of reaction.
  • Some reactions are restricted to the oral mucosa, especially with dental amalgam fillings, and are linked to metals such as mercury, gold, cobalt, or nickel.
  • Lichenoid eruptions usually arise within months to years of starting the causative drug and may take equally long to resolve after stopping it.
  • Histologically, they show inflammation along the dermo-epidermal junction, keratinocyte necrosis, and lymphocytic infiltrates.
  • The histology closely resembles idiopathic lichen planus, though eosinophils may help suggest a drug-induced cause.
  • Corticosteroids can be used if the drug cannot be discontinued.

Explanation of other options:

Ciprofloxacin (Option A): Ciprofloxacin mainly causes tendinopathy, central nervous system toxicity, and peripheral neuropathy.

Fluconazole (Option B): Fluconazole is used to treat candidiasis and adverse effects include skin rash, reversible alopecia, and, in some cases, hepatotoxicity.

Lithium (Option D): Lithium can cause cutaneous lichenoid eruptions and worsen psoriasis, while in the mouth, it more often causes dryness and taste changes; oral lichenoid lesions are rare.

question_text: An 80-year-old woman consumed a drug that inhibits Na+-Cl- cotransporters in the distal convoluted tubule in excess. Serum studies are most likely to show which of the following sets of findings?
explanation:
• Inhibition of Na+-Cl- cotransporters in the early distal convoluted tubule is the mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics, which are used to treat hypertension, a common comorbidity in elderly patients.
  • Inhibition of Na+-Cl- cotransporters in the early DCT can cause hyponatremia due to increased Na+ excretion. Inhibition of Na+ reabsorption by the early DCT also increases Na+ delivery to the late DCT and early collecting tubule, which can cause hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis due to increased K+ and H+ secretion in exchange for luminal Na+ reabsorption. It also causeshypercalcemia due in part to increased Ca2+ reabsorption at the proximal tubule as a result of increased extracellular fluid reabsorption in this segment.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 267

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman is presented with periorbital edema, a maculopapular rash on her chest, and a fever of 101F. She has a history of hypertension, diabetes, and osteoarthritis. Laboratory studies of serum show:
1. Sodium = 139 mEq/L
2. Potassium = 4.8 mEq/L
3. Chloride = 100 mEg/L
4. Bicarbonate = 24 mEq/L
5. BUN =58 mg/dL
6. Creatinine = 3.1 mg/dL
Urinalysis shows mild proteinuria and eosinophils. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the findings seen in this patient?
explanation:
• Acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) is caused by an acute inflammation of the renal interstitium and is most likely related to a hypersensitivity reaction. This condition is usually caused by a drug. Examples of drugs producing this condition include nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen and indomethacin; antibiotics such as penicillins, cephalosporins, and sulfonamides; diuretics such as furosemide and thiazides; and other drugs such as phenytoin, cimetidine, allopurinol, and proton pump inhibitors.
  • The typical presentation for acute interstitial nephritis is the development of oliguria, fever, and rash that starts days to weeks after starting the drug. Eosinophils are seen in the urine. This can progress to renal papillary necrosis. Treatment consists primarily of supportive measures and removal of the inciting agent, as well as corticosteroids, such as prednisone.
  • Note that in addition to acute interstitial nephritis, NSAIDs can also produce hemodynamically-mediated renal failure because of the reduction of prostaglandin synthesis. Renal prostaglandins cause vasodilation. Normally, they do not have much influence on renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate, so in a healthy individual, NSAIDs likely have minimal effect on renal function.
  • However, in edematous or volume-depleted states, these prostaglandins compensate for angiotensin- or epinephrine-induced renal vasoconstriction. The blockade of prostaglandin production by NSAIDs in these conditions, can lead to unopposed vasoconstriction and acute renal failure. Risk factors include diabetes, heart failure, cirrhosis, dehydration, blood or fluid loss, and being elderly.

Reference : Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 260

question_text: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is on Indomethacin for pain management. He is also initiated on an ACE inhibitor for newly diagnosed hypertension. What is the most likely adverse effect of this drug combination?
explanation:
Explanation:

Adverse Effects of Captopril

  • Hypotension:
    • Sudden fall in blood pressure, especially in patients on diuretics or with congestive heart failure (CHF).
  • Hyperkalemia:
    • More likely in patients with renal impairment or those taking potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, or β-blockers.
  • Cough:
    • Persistent, dry, brassy cough typically appearing within 1-8 weeks of therapy.
  • Skin Reactions:
    • Rashes and urticaria.
    • Angioedema is a rare but serious complication.
  • Dysgeusia:
    • Reversible loss or alteration of taste sensation.
  • Foetopathy:
    • When used in the second or third trimester of pregnancy, may cause fetal growth retardation, organ hypoplasia, or fetal death.
  • Gastrointestinal and CNS Symptoms:
    • Headache, dizziness, nausea, and bowel disturbances.
  • Hematologic and Renal Effects:
    • Granulocytopenia, proteinuria.
    • Acute renal failure may occur, particularly in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis due to reduced glomerular filtration pressure.

Explanation of other options: Incorrect Choices Explanation

Hyponatremia (Option B):

  • Incorrect, as ACE inhibitors do not cause significant sodium loss.
  • Thiazide diuretics, rather than NSAIDs or ACE inhibitors, are a more common cause of hyponatremia.

Hyperuricemia (Option C):

  • Incorrect, as indomethacin and NSAIDs can impair uric acid excretion, but ACE inhibitors do not contribute significantly to hyperuricemia.
  • Thiazide and loop diuretics are more strongly associated with hyperuricemia.

Hypercalcemia (Option D):

  • Incorrect, as neither NSAIDs nor ACE inhibitors significantly affect calcium levels.
  • Thiazide diuretics are more likely to cause hypercalcemia.

Key Takeaways:

Hyperkalemia is likely in patients with impaired renal function and in those taking K+ sparing diuretics, NSAIDs or β blockers.

question_text:
Which of the following sentences are TRUE for Methylxanthines?
1. They have positive chronotropic and inotropic effects on heart.
2. They inhibit the secretion of gastric acid and digestive enzymes.
3. They are weak diuretics but have no therapeutic significance
4. They reverse fatigue of diaphragm in patient with COPD
5. They cause bronchoconstriction.
explanation:
• The methylxanthines have positive chronotropic and inotropic effects.
  • At low concentrations, these effects appear to result from inhibition of presynaptic adenosine receptors in sympathetic nerves increasing catecholamine release at nerve endings.
  • The higher concentrations (> 10 μmol/L, 2 mg/L) associated with inhibition of phosphodiesterase and increases in cAMP may result in increased influx of calcium.
  • At much higher concentrations (> 100 μmol/L), sequestration of calcium by the sarcoplasmic reticulum is impaired.
  • The methylxanthines stimulate secretion of both gastric acid and digestive enzymes.
  • The methylxanthines—especially theophylline—are weak diuretics.
  • This effect may involve both increased glomerular filtration and reduced tubular sodium reabsorption.
  • The diuresis is not of sufficient magnitude to be therapeutically useful.
  • The bronchodilation produced by the methylxanthines is the major therapeutic action in asthma.
  • Tolerance does not develop, but adverse effects, especially in the central nervous system, may limit the dose.
  • In addition to their effect on airway smooth muscle, these agents—in sufficient concentration—inhibit antigen-induced release of histamine from lung tissue; their effect on mucociliary transport is unknown.
  • The respiratory actions of the methylxanthines may not be confined to the airways, for they also strengthen the contractions of isolated skeletal muscle in vitro and improve contractility and reverse fatigue of the diaphragm in patients with COPD.
  • This effect on diaphragmatic performance—rather than an effect on the respiratory center—may account for theophylline’s ability to improve the ventilator response to hypoxia and to diminish dyspnea even in patients with irreversible airflow obstruction.

Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 20- Drugs used in asthma by Dr. Homer A. Boushy, MD. Page no. 345,346

question_text: A group is traveling to the mountains when a girl begins experiencing symptoms of altitude sickness. What is the preferred medication to treat her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The preferred drug for both preventing and treating acute mountain sickness (AMS) is acetazolamide. This medication is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that works primarily in the proximal convoluted tubule, promoting the excretion of sodium and bicarbonate (Na+/HCO2) in the urine.

At high altitudes, reduced oxygen levels trigger hyperventilation, which leads to excessive loss of CO2 and results in respiratory alkalosis. This alkalosis suppresses the central nervous system, contributing to symptoms such as headache, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, and shortness of breath.

By causing a mild metabolic acidosis, acetazolamide helps counteract respiratory alkalosis, thereby reducing hyperventilation and alleviating symptoms of mountain sickness.

Explanation for other options:

Promethazine (Option A): Promethazine is an antihistamine commonly used to treat motion sickness, nausea, and vertigo. While it may help relieve symptoms like nausea and dizziness associated with mountain sickness, it does not address the underlying acclimatization problems responsible for acute mountain sickness (AMS).

Dimenhydrinate (Option C): Dimenhydrinate is another antihistamine used for motion sickness and nausea. Similar to promethazine, it can alleviate symptoms but does not prevent or treat the fundamental cause of mountain sickness.

Thiazide Diuretics (Option D): Thiazides are mainly prescribed for hypertension and edema management. They have no role in the prevention or treatment of mountain sickness and do not aid in altitude acclimatization.

question_text: Identify the incorrect choice regarding choice of anti-arrhythmic.
option_a: A 12-year-old with congenital LQTS = Magnesium sulphate
option_c: A 67-year-old on digoxin with supraventricular arrythmia = Propranolol
option_d: A 56-year old with ventricular arrhythmia due after MI = lidocaine
explanation:
Other choices are correct

A 45-year-old with supraventricular arrhythmia = Verapamil

A 67-year-old on digoxin with supraventricular arrythmia = Propranolol

A 56-year old with ventricular arrhythmia due after MI = lidocaine

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 248

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and requires prophylaxis for the same. Which of the following drugs is appropriate for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, verapamil is appropriate for the prophylaxis of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia.

Verapamil

Mechanism:

  • Blocks L-type Ca²&sup+; channels in the AV node.
  • Slows AV nodal conduction and increases the refractory period.
  • Interrupts the re-entry circuit commonly responsible for PSVT.

Use:

  • Effective in terminating AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT), the most common form of PSVT.
  • Given intravenously for acute termination and orally for prophylaxis of PSVT.
  • Prophylaxis of migraine
  • Improves left ventricular outflow obstruction in patients with hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

Contraindications:

  • Avoid in WPW syndrome with atrial fibrillation (can worsen conduction via accessory pathway).
  • Contraindicated in severe LV dysfunction, hypotension, or heart block.

Explanation of other options:

IV adenosine (Option A): It is used acutely to terminate PSVT but not for prophylaxis since it has a very short half-life of about 10 seconds.

IV esmolol (Option B): It is an ultra-short-acting beta-blocker, used acutely often in intraoperative or critical care settings, but it is not suitable for chronic prophylaxis.

Oral phenytoin (Option C): It is an anti-epileptic that may have anti-arrhythmic properties in digitalis toxicity, but it is not used in PSVT prophylaxis.

question_text: 56-year-old woman presents with complaints of fatigue, sluggishness, and weight gain. She has been taking T4 since 5 years without significant problems regarding her energy level. Her recent history is significant for diagnosis of arrhythmia, and she is currently taking an anti-arrhythmic drug. What is the most likely cause of her current condition?
explanation:
• Amiodarone is an iodine-containing anti-arrhythmic drug with complex effects on the thyroid gland and thyroid hormones.
    • One of its actions is to inhibit peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
    • Note that propranolol also reduces conversion of T4 to T3.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 692

question_text: In the given cardiac action potential graph, identify the phase where amiodarone acts.
explanation:
Explanation:

Amiodarone is a class III anti-arrhythmic agents, which act on phase 3 of the cardiac action potential, which is the repolarisation phase.

  • Amiodarone is a structural analogue of thyroid hormone with multiple electrophysiological effects.
  • Blocks inactivated Na+ channels, decreases Ca²+ current, prolongs PR, QRS, and QT intervals, and delays repolarisation by blocking K+ channels. (Options A, B, and C ruled out)

question_text: The dotted line in the diagram represents an action potential following the infusion of a pharmacological agent into cardiomyocytes. Which antiarrhythmic agent is most likely responsible?
explanation:
The graph shows a ventricular action potential. The drug changes the duration of the rapid upstroke of the action potential (phase O) without significantly changing the overall duration of the action potential shows the effect of class IC antiarrhythmics. It acts by slow opening of voltage-gated sodium channels and decrease the slope of phase 0 while still maintaining the AP duration. Class IC antiarrhythmics also exhibit use dependence, further decreasing the slope as heart rate increases.

Although both class IA (Option D : Quinidine) and IB (Option B : Lidocaine) also slow opening of voltage-gated sodium channels and decrease the slope of phase 0, they prolong and shorten the AP duration, respectively.

Option A : Verapamil, a non-DHP CCB, class 4 drug, effective in arrhythmias that must traverse calcium-dependent cardiac tissue such as the AV node. Here, experiment is done on cardiac myocyte and AP shown is of also cardiac myocyte not pacemaker. Thus it cannot be an answer.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 239

question_text: A 70-year-old female presents to the ED with a racing heartbeat. She is subsequently placed on continuous ECG monitor and irregular rhythm is seen. The diagnosis of atrial fibrillation is made. She is started on an amiodarone drip. What side effect you should be aware of when starting amiodarone?
explanation:
Amiodarone has several well-known side effects, including pulmonary fibrosis, hepatotoxicity, and thyroid imbalances. For this reason, pulmonary function tests, liver function tests, and thyroid function tests should be monitored while taking amiodarone.


  • Blurry yellow vision is common side effect of digoxin toxicity, not amiodarone. However, blurry vision can be due to corneal micro-deposition of amiodarone.
  • Lupus-like syndrome is a common side effect of sulphonamide, hydralazine, isoniazid, procainamide (SHIP), can presented with malar rash, anti-histone antibody+, which is reversible with drug discontinuation.
  • Prolongation of the AV refractory period is a common side effect of class Ic antiarrhythmics, such as flecainide and propafenone, not amiodarone.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 243

question_text: Which of the following drugs is correctly paired with its ECG effects?
option_a: Quinidine: Increased PR and decreased QT interval
option_d: Lidocaine: Decreased QRS and PR interval
explanation:
Anti-arrhythmic drugs are used to prevent recurrent arrhythmias and restore sinus rhythm in patients with cardiac arrhythmias. These drugs are classified based on their electrophysiological effect on the myocardium.

GROUP 1 ANTIARRHYTHMICS (SODIUM CHANNEL BLOCKERS)

The group 1 drugs have local anesthetic actions and slow the upstroke of sodium-dependent action potentials and usually prolong QRS duration in ischemic and depolarized cells and slow or abolish abnormal pacemakers wherever these processes depend on sodium channels. They are further subdivided on the basis of their effects on AP duration


GROUP 2 ANTIARRHYTHMICS (BETA BLOCKERS)

Propranolol and esmolol are prototypic anti-arrhythmic β blockers. Their mechanism in arrhythmias is primarily cardiac β-adrenoceptor blockade and reduction in cAMP, which results in a modest reduction of both sodium and calcium currents and the suppression of abnormal pacemakers. The AV node is particularly sensitive to β blockers and the PR interval is usually prolonged.

Esmolol, a very short-acting β blocker for intravenous administration, is used exclusively in acute arrhythmias. Propranolol and metoprolol, are commonly used chronically to prevent arrhythmias in patients who have had a myocardial infarction.


GROUP 3 ANTIARRHYTHMICS (POTASSIUM IK CHANNEL BLOCKERS)

  • Dofetilide and ibutilide are typical group 3 drugs.
  • Sotalol is a chiral compound (ie, it has 2 optical isomers). One isomer is an effective β blocker, and both isomers contribute to the anti-arrhythmic action through K-channel block. The clinical preparation contains both isomers.
  • Amiodarone is useful in most types of arrhythmias and is considered the most efficacious of all anti-arrhythmic drugs. This may be because it has a broad spectrum of action: It blocks sodium, calcium, and potassium channels and β adrenoceptors.
  • Dronedarone, an amiodarone analog, is also approved. Like amiodarone, it acts on sodium, potassium, and calcium channels, but at present it is approved only for the treatment of atrial fibrillation or flutter. Dronedarone does not appear to be as efficacious as amiodarone but may be less toxic.

GROUP 4 ANTIARRHYTHMICS (CALCIUM L-TYPE CHANNEL BLOCKERS)

Verapamil is the prototype. Diltiazem is also an effective anti-arrhythmic drug.



Properties of the prototype anti-arrhythmic drugs Correct option :

Flecainide, class 1c drug, no effect on ventricular AP duration or the QT interval. However, They are powerful depressants of sodium current, and can markedly slow conduction velocity in atrial and ventricular cells. Thus, They increase the QRS duration of the ECG is true statement.

Incorrect options :

(A) Quinidine, class 1a drug, block Na and therefore slow conduction velocity in the atria, Purkinje fibers, and ventricular cells leading to increase QRS duration and QT interval, thus decreased QT intervals is false. Increased PR is partly true because increase owing to channel-blocking action but as PR interval may decrease owing to antimuscarinic action.

(C) Verapamil, a non-DHP CCB, class 4 drug, effective in arrhythmias that must traverse calcium-dependent cardiac tissue such as the AV node. AV conduction velocity is decreased, and effective refractory period and PR interval are increased. Thus, Decreased PR interval is wrong statement.

(D) Lidocaine, class 1b drug, selectively affect ischemic or depolarized Purkinje and ventricular tissue and have little effect on atrial tissue; the drugs reduce AP duration in some cells (possibly by blocking the late, slowly inactivating Na+ current). Because they slow recovery of sodium channels from inactivation, 1B drugs do not shorten (and may even prolong) the effective refractory period. Because these agents have little effect on normal cardiac cells, they have little effect on the ECG. Here, Decreased QRS and PR interval is incorrect option.

(E) Metoprolol, a cardio selective beta-blocker is class 2 drug. The AV node is particularly sensitive to β blockers and the PR interval is usually prolonged by group 2 drugs not QRS duration.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 239

question_text: A 48-year old male had an overdose, and manifested severe acute procainamide toxicity with markedly long QT. Which of the following should be given immediately?
explanation:
The most effective therapy for procainamide (and quinidine) toxicity appears to be concentrated sodium lactate due to increase in sodium current by increasing the sodium ion gradient and reduced drug-receptor binding by alkalinizing the tissue. Pressor sympathomimetics are to be used to reverse drug-induced hypotension if indicated.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, 14th Edition, Page Number-241.

question_text: A 68-year-old woman comes to the ED with chest pain radiating to left shoulder. Her ECG reveals ventricular tachycardia with ST-segment elevation. Trop C levels are markedly increased. A diagnosis of myocardial infarction is made. Her arrhythmia will probably be treated initially with
explanation:
Given clinical scenario of chest pain with ST-segment elevation and Trop C elevation suggests myocardial damage, complicated by ventricular tachycardia, a common cause of death in MI patients in the first 24 hours.

Option C : Lidocaine has limited applications as an anti-arrhythmic drug, but emergency treatment of myocardial infarction arrhythmias is one of the most important. Lidocaine is also useful in digoxin-induced arrhythmias. After recovery from the acute phase of a myocardial infarction, β blockers are used for 2 years or more to prevent sudden death arrhythmia. Procainamide or amiodarone are used as alternative drugs in this situation.

Option A : Adenosine, markedly slows or completely blocks conduction in the atrioventricular node, probably by hyperpolarizing the tissue (through increased IK) and by reducing calcium current. Adenosine is extremely effective in abolishing AV nodal arrhythmia, and because of its very low toxicity it has become the drug of choice for this arrhythmia but its not used in ventricular arrhythmias.

Option B : Digoxin, is used to reduce the conduction velocity or increase the refractory period of the AV node, so that ventricular rate is controlled within a range compatible with efficient filling and ejection, in atrial flutter and fibrillation, not for ventricular arrhythmia.

Option D : Quinidine, can be used for PSVT (AVNRT and AVRT) and Ectopic SVTs, but less preferred in VTs. Quinidine (the optical isomer of quinine) causes cinchonism (headache, vertigo, tinnitus); cardiac depression; gastrointestinal upset; and autoimmune reactions (eg; thrombocytopenic purpura).

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 244

question_text: You admit a patient and instruct the nurse in-charge to continuously monitor ECG every 4 hours since you gave a drug that can cause a potent change in the ECG. Which of the following medications can cause a prolongation of the QT interval?
explanation:

  7. Prokinetic : Cisapride

question_text: Which of the following side effects is least commonly linked to the use of amiodarone?
explanation:
Explanation:

Amiodarone is a powerful antiarrhythmic medication mainly used to treat ventricular arrhythmias and atrial fibrillation. Although it is associated with numerous side effects and has a long half-life, gynecomastia is not typically considered a common adverse effect.

question_text: An anesthetist injected bupivacaine in a patient for axillary nerve block. Later, the patient developed restlessness, agitation and cardiovascular collapse. Next best step in the management would be?
explanation:
Bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic local anaesthetic

  • Diazepam is used to treat convulsions. If not responding, thiopentone may be used.
  • Arrhythmias should be promptly treated using bretylium, amiodarone, disopyramide, magnesium sulphate, esmolol or sotalol.

  • In refractory arrhythmias, intravenous lipid emulsion (like intralipid)has been found to be extremely useful.
  • Bupivacaine induced cardiotoxicity is enhanced by acidosis, hypercarbia and hypoxemia.

question_text: What ECG changes are associated with the use of the anti-tubercular drug bedaquiline?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bedaquiline is an antitubercular medication used to treat multidrug-resistant tuberculosis. The most notable and clinically important side effect of bedaquiline is QT interval prolongation on the ECG.

Bedaquiline

  • Mechanism of Action (MOA):
    • Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, an essential enzyme for energy production in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
    • Disrupts energy production, leading to bacterial death.
  • Reactions:
    • Cross-resistance occurs with clofazimine.
  • Metabolism:
    • Metabolized by CYP3A4 enzyme.
    • Rifampicin, a CYP3A4 inducer, decreases bedaquiline's effectiveness.
  • Side Effects:
    • Common: Nausea and diarrhea.
    • Serious: QT interval prolongation on ECG.

Explanation for other options:

PR interval prolongation (Option B): is typically linked to drugs that slow AV nodal conduction, such as beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, or digoxin, and is not associated with bedaquiline.

QRS widening (Option C): usually results from class 1 antiarrhythmic drugs and is related to conduction abnormalities or bundle branch blocks; however, bedaquiline does not cause this effect.

ST-segment elevation (Option D): is seen with sodium channel blockers and during acute myocardial infarction (MI), but it is not a recognized side effect of bedaquiline.

question_text: Which of the following sets of drug interaction and mechanism is accurately described?
option_a: Ibuprofen and warfarin: increased risk of GI bleeding; ibuprofen inhibition of CYP2C9
option_b: Sotalol and furosemide: increased risk of QT prolongation and torsades de pointes; furosemide induced inhibition of CYP3A4
option_c: Sildenafil and sublingual nitroglycerin: increased risk of hypotension; sildenafil inhibition of the PDE- 5 that inactivates cyclic guanosine monophosphate
option_d: Ritonavir and lovastatin: increased risk of myotoxicity; ritonavir inhibition of CYP2C19
explanation:
Sildenafil and nitroglycerin should not be co-prescribed. The pharmacologic effects of sildenafil result from inhibition of the PDE-5 that inactivates GMP in the vasculature. Nitroglycerin and related nitrates used to treat angina produce vasodilation by elevating cyclic GMP. Thus, co- administration of these nitrates with sildenafil can cause profound hypotension, which can be catastrophic in patients with coronary disease.

NSAIDs cause gastric ulcers, and in patients treated with warfarin, the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding is increased almost threefold by concomitant use of an NSAID such as ibuprofen. This is not mediated by inhibition of a cytochrome P450 enzyme (option A).

Torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia during administration of QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics (quinidine, sotalol, dofetilide) occurs much more frequently in patients receiving diuretics, probably reflecting hypokalemia instead of inhibition of any cytochrome P450 enzyme (option B).

Ritonavir is a powerful inhibitor of CYP3A4 (not 2C19) (option D) and should not be co- prescribed with lovastatin.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 62

question_text: A 53-year-old obese man with past history of acute myocardial infarction is on metoprolol and low- dose aspirin. His total serum cholesterol level is 155 mg/dL, with an HDL level of 27 mg/dL and a triglyceride level of 92 mg/dL. Which of the following lipid-lowering agents would be most effective for preventing future cardiovascular events in this patient?
explanation:
• Patients with low high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels (men <40 mg/dL, women <50 mg/dL) are at increased risk for cardiovascular disease. HDL is involved in reverse cholesterol transport; it helps to remove cholesterol from peripheral tissues and transports it to the liver for metabolism. This is accomplished through 2 different pathways. In the direct pathway, HDL delivers cholesterol esters directly to the liver via a scavenger receptor (SCARB1) on the hepatocyte cell membrane. In the indirect pathway, the cholesterol in HDL is transferred to low-density lipoprotein (LDL) and very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL) by the cholesterol ester transfer protein.
  • Nonpharmacologic measures such as exercise, weight loss, and smoking cessation help to raise HDL levels and have significant cardiovascular benefits. In contrast, use of medications to raise HDL levels does not improve cardiovascular outcomes. Pharmacologic treatment of patients with low HDL levels should focus on lowering LDL cholesterol with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins), as these are the most effective lipid- lowering drugs for preventing cardiovascular events. Statins are indicated for secondary prevention in all patients with known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, regardless of baseline lipid levels.
  • Cationic exchange resin = cholestyramine
  • Essential fatty acids = Omega-3-fatty acid
  • Pharmacologic vitamin= niacin

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 221

question_text: Which of the following is a PCSK9 inhibitor?
explanation:
Explanation:

Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor that helps lower LDL cholesterol levels by blocking the PCSK9 enzyme. This inhibition increases the number of available LDL receptors on hepatocytes, enhancing LDL uptake from the bloodstream and thereby reducing plasma LDL cholesterol concentrations.

Newer hypolipidemic drugs:

Ezetimibe (Option C Ruled Out):

  • Inhibits the intestinal absorption of cholesterol and phytosterols by interfering with the NPC1L1 transporter in the small intestine.
  • Commonly used alongside statins to manage primary hypercholesterolemia.
  • Should not be combined with bile acid sequestrants, as they reduce the absorption and effectiveness of ezetimibe.

PCSK9 inhibitors:

  • These monoclonal antibodies block PCSK9, enhancing LDL receptor recycling and increasing the removal of LDL cholesterol from circulation.
  • Alirocumab and Evolocumab significantly reduce LDL-C levels in familial hypercholesterolemia or established cardiovascular disease.
  • Administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks or monthly and used as adjuncts to statin therapy.
  • Inclisiran is a novel small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy that silences the PCSK9 gene to achieve a similar LDL-lowering effect.

Lomitapide (Option B Ruled Out):

  • Inhibits microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP).
  • This reduces the formation of VLDL in hepatocytes and chylomicrons in enterocytes, thereby lowering lipid levels.

Omega-3 fatty acids:

  • Naturally found in fish oils.
  • Reduce free fatty acid (FFA) delivery to the liver and inhibit triglyceride-synthesizing enzymes, leading to decreased hepatic VLDL production.
  • Common formulations include Eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA; Icosapent) and Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

Bempedoic acid (Option D Ruled Out):

  • A prodrug that is converted to its active form, bempedoic acid-CoA.
  • Competitively inhibits ATP citrate lyase, an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol synthesis pathway.
  • This inhibition decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis by reducing acetyl-CoA availability to HMG-CoA reductase.

question_text:
A 36-year-old man comes for regular check-up. His lab report shown below.
Total cholesterol= 290 mg/dL
HDL = 45 mg/dL
LDL =110 mg/dL
Triglycerides = 675 mg/dL
He is started on fenofibrate therapy. This medication is most likely to help the patient by which of the following mechanisms?
explanation:
• This patient has a moderately elevated (>500 mg/dL) triglyceride level, which is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Lifestyle modifications (increased aerobic exercise, decreased alcohol and total caloric intake) can decrease triglycerides, but moderate (or worse) hypertriglyceridemia usually requires pharmacologic therapy. Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL to release free fatty acids, which can be used for energy or converted back to triglycerides for storage in adipose tissue. It also facilitates the transfer of triglycerides from these lipoproteins to HDL.
  • Fibrates (eg, gemfibrozil, fenofibrate) activate peroxisome proliferator activated receptor alpha (PPAR-a), which leads to decreased hepatic VLDL production and increased LPL activity. They are able to decrease triglyceride levels by 25%-50% and increase HDL by 5%-20%. Fish oil supplements containing high concentrations of omega-3 fatty acids also decrease VLDL production, and inhibit synthesis of apolipoprotein B as well. These supplements lower triglycerides and can be used as na alternate treatment for patients with moderate hypertriglyceridemia.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 218

question_text: Which of the following drugs stimulates PPAR-alpha?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gemfibrozil is a fibrate (fibric acid derivative) that works by activating PPAR-alpha (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha).

Explanations of other options:

Ezetimibe (Option B): Ezetimibe is a cholesterol absorption blocker that prevents dietary cholesterol uptake in the small intestine by inhibiting the PCIL1 transporter. It is commonly combined with statins in the treatment of primary hypercholesterolemia.

Colestipol (Option C): Colestipol is a bile acid sequestrant that attaches to bile acids in the intestine, blocking their reabsorption and enhancing their elimination through feces. It is used as an add-on therapy alongside statins.

Simvastatin (Option D): Simvastatin is a statin which acts by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, that lowers cholesterol levels by blocking its synthesis in the liver.

question_text: Which of the following drugs is most effective at lowering LDL cholesterol levels?
explanation:
Explanation:

Statins, such as atorvastatin and rosuvastatin, are the most effective drugs for lowering LDL cholesterol.

They work by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme involved in cholesterol synthesis in the liver. This inhibition reduces cholesterol production and increases LDL receptor activity, which helps clear LDL cholesterol from the bloodstream.

Among statins, rosuvastatin is the most potent and efficacious, with a longer duration of action compared to atorvastatin.

Atorvastatin is considered safer for use in patients with renal failure.

Explanation for other options:

Niacin (Option A): also known as Vitamin B3 or nicotinic acid, works by inhibiting lipolysis in adipose tissue and reducing triglyceride production in the liver. It also increases HDL cholesterol levels.

Fibrates (Option B): activate peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR-α), which lowers triglyceride production, raises HDL cholesterol levels, and decreases hepatic triglyceride synthesis.

Resins (Option D): including cholestyramine, colestipol, and colesevelam, are often used alongside statin therapy and are considered safe for use during pregnancy.

question_text: 68-year-old man has achy pain in thigh that is not related to activity. The patient has tried warm compresses. Physical examination shows diffuse tenderness in the proximal muscles of the upper and lower extremities. Serum creatine kinase activity is elevated. Which of the following drug combinations is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation:
• Statins (eg, atorvastatin) are the first-line therapy for most patients with hypercholesterolemia and are useful in primary and secondary prevention of acute coronary events. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme responsible for the rate-limiting step in synthesis of cholesterol. Statins lower total cholesterol, LDL, and triglyceride levels. The primary side effects of statins include myopathy and hepatitis.
    • Statin-associated myopathy is usually characterized by mild muscular pain and resolves with discontinuation of the medication. However, some patients will develop severe myopathy with striking elevations in creatine kinase levels and occasional rhabdomyolysis. The risk of severe myopathy is increased when statins are given concurrently with fibrates (particularly gemfibrozil), which impair the hepatic clearance of statins and lead to excessive blood levels. An increased risk of statin myopathy is also likely with concurrent use of niacin or ezetimibe, but to a lesser extent.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 212

question_text: A 45-year-old man with dyslipidaemia. He is started on simvastatin and cholestyramine. Which of the following best describes the independent effects of simvastatin and cholestyramine, respectively, on hepatic cholesterol synthesis?
explanation:
• Bile acids are synthesized in the liver from cholesterol catabolism. Bile enters the duodenum through gallbladder contraction. Bile acids are primarily absorbed in the terminal ileum, with the small amount that remains unabsorbed being excreted in the stool (this amount is matched by bile acid synthesis)
  • Statins are the first-line therapy for most patients with hypercholesterolemia. These drugs competitively inhibit HMG CoA reductase, the enzyme responsible for the conversion of HMG CoA to mevalonate (ie, the rate-limiting step in hepatic cholesterol synthesis). This inhibition decreases hepatic cholesterol synthesis. The resulting upregulation of LDL receptors causes increased uptake of LDL from the circulation. Statins are very effective in reducing LDL cholesterol. Statins' effects on triglyceride and HDL levels are comparatively modest.
  • Bile acid-binding resins (ie, bile acid sequestrants) work by binding bile acids in the gastrointestinal tract, thereby interfering with the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids and causing increased bile acid excretion. This results in hepatic synthesis of new bile acids, a process that consumes liver cholesterol stores. Hepatic uptake of LDL from the circulation is increased for continued bile acid synthesis. Bile acid production and secretion are increased by 10-fold due to this interruption of the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids. Hepatic cholesterol reduction is an activating factor for HMG CoA reductase and subsequently results in increased hepatic cholesterol synthesis. This effect can be blocked with the addition of a statin drug to the treatment regimen, leading to a greater reduction in LDL levels than with use of either drug alone (synergistic action).

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 1097

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a history of hyperlipidemia was started on statin therapy for high triglyceride levels. However, his triglycerides remain above 600 mg/dL despite treatment. Which of the following medications should be added next to help control his triglyceride levels?
explanation:
Explanation:

Fibrates, such as gemfibrozil and fenofibrate, are the most effective medications for reducing triglyceride levels.

They work by activating PPAR-α, which increases the expression of genes involved in breaking down triglycerides and clearing VLDL from the bloodstream.

As a result, fibrates lower triglyceride levels and raise HDL cholesterol levels.

Explanation for other options:

Niacin (Option B): also known as Vitamin B3 or nicotinic acid, works by inhibiting lipolysis in adipose tissue. It can lower triglycerides and raise HDL cholesterol but is less effective than fibrates for reducing triglyceride levels.

Statins (Option C): primarily target lowering LDL cholesterol and have only a modest impact on triglycerides. Since this patient's triglycerides remain high despite statin use, adding a fibrate would be a more suitable option.

Resins (Option D): which include cholestyramine, colestipol, and colesevelam, are typically used alongside statins and are considered safe during pregnancy.

question_text:
A patient who has recently had a myocardial infarction (MI) presents for a follow-up. His cholesterol levels are as follows: total cholesterol 238 mg/dL, triglycerides 125 mg/dL, and HDL 50 mg/dL. He is currently taking atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin. Which of the following medications should be added to his regimen?
1. Ezetimibe
2. Bempedoic acid
3. Evolocumab
4. Gemfibrozil
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has elevated LDL cholesterol post-MI despite statin therapy. Therefore, Ezetimibe, Bempedoic acid, and Evolocumab can be added for further LDL reduction.
Gemfibrozil is not indicated since triglycerides are normal.

  • Ezetimibe (1): Inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption → ↓ LDL and total cholesterol.
  • Bempedoic acid (2): Inhibits ATP-citrate lyase → ↓ hepatic cholesterol synthesis → ↓ LDL.
  • Evolocumab (3): PCSK9 inhibitor → prevents LDL receptor degradation → ↑ LDL clearance.

Explanation of other options:

Gemfibrozil (Option D): Incorrect because it is used for severe hypertriglyceridemia and not for LDL lowering.

Key Takeaways:

  • Add Ezetimibe, Bempedoic acid, or Evolocumab if LDL remains high despite statins.
  • Gemfibrozil reserved for hypertriglyceridemia.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors are potent LDL reducers post-MI.

question_text: A 57-year-old male is admitted due to muscle pain, fatigue and dark urine. Current medications include metoprolol, atorvastatin, and aspirin. Laboratory evaluation reveals that he is in acute renal failure. The addition of which of the following medications is most likely to have precipitated this patient's condition?
explanation:
• Statins are very effective agents in the reduction of LDL cholesterol. Serious side effects of statins include myopathy and hepatitis. Myopathy is a rare complication of statin use, clinically defined as muscle pain with serum creatine kinase over 10 times the upper limit of normal. With the exception of pravastatin, the statin drugs (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin) are metabolized by the liver CYP3A4.
  • Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4. Thus, concurrent use of erythromycin with these drugs causes increased serum levels of statin, which is in turn associated with increased risk for myopathy. Other macrolides, such as clarithromycin, also inhibit CYP3A4. Azithromycin, however, does not have a significant effect on CYP3A4. Other inhibitors of cytochrome CYP3A4 include ketoconazole, cyclosporine, HIV protease inhibitors, and grapefruit juice. If a patient is on an agent that inhibits CYP3A4, pravastatin is the statin of choice.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 211

question_text: A patient being treated for hypertriglyceridemia develops flushing, gout, and elevated liver enzymes after starting medication. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these side effects?
explanation:
Explanation:

Niacin (Nicotinamide) is commonly used to lower triglycerides and raise HDL cholesterol & is associated with side effects like flushing, gout & elevated liver enzymes. 

Niacin: 

Niacin is Vitamin B3 or nicotinic acid. It inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue and ￬triglyceride production by the liver. It also increases HDL levels. Its use is limited by its side effects:

  • Flushing (taking aspirin before niacin helps to reduce flushing)
  • Dry skin
  • Dyspepsia
  • Hepatotoxicity presents with fatigue and weakness
  • Hyperglycemia- it can indicate insulin resistance and should be used cautiously in those with diabetes
  • Increases uric acid levels, hence contraindicated in gout

Explanation for other options:

Atorvastatin (Option B) is a statin used primarily to lower LDL cholesterol and triglycerides. While it can cause elevated liver enzymes and muscle-related issues (such as myopathy), it is not typically associated with flushing or gout.

Fenofibrate (Option C) is a fibrate that effectively lowers triglycerides. It can lead to elevated liver enzymes and muscle-related side effects, but flushing and gout are not commonly associated with its use.

Cholestyramine (Option D) is a bile acid sequestrant used to lower LDL cholesterol. It is mainly known to cause gastrointestinal issues like constipation, but it does not cause flushing, gout, or elevated liver enzymes.

question_text: Which of the following drugs should be avoided in a patient on rosuvastatin therapy?
explanation:
Clarithromycin being a CYP enzyme inhibitor, can cause Statin toxicity due to lack of metabolism.

All statins are remarkably well tolerated; overall incidence of side effects not differing from placebo.

Muscle aches are the commonest (10%) side effect. Rise in CPK levels occurs infrequently. Myopathy is the only serious reaction, but is rare (< 1 per 1000). Few fatalities due to rhabdomyolysis are on record.

Myopathy and liver injury is more common when nicotinic acid/gemfibrozil or CYP3A4 inhibitor-ketoconazole/erythromycin/ Clarithromycin/cyclosporine/HIV protease inhibitor is given concurrently.

question_text: Which of the following drugs is a PCSK9 inhibitor?
explanation:
Explanation:

Evolocumab, a monoclonal antibody, is a PCSK9 inhibitor employed in managing elevated cholesterol levels.

PCSK9 inhibitors:

  • These drugs act on PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9), a protein that limits the liver's capacity to clear LDL cholesterol ("bad" cholesterol) from circulation.
  • Elevated LDL cholesterol is considered harmful because it plays a major role in the development of cardiovascular disease.
  • Normally, LDL receptors on liver cells recycle to the surface to remove LDL from the blood, but when PCSK9 binds to these receptors, it blocks their recycling.
  • As a result, LDL accumulates in the bloodstream, raising the risk of heart disease.
  • Evolocumab is given as a subcutaneous injection every 2-4 weeks, based on dosage and patient response.
  • It is commonly prescribed alongside other lipid-lowering agents, like statins, for patients who are unable to achieve target LDL cholesterol levels through diet and exercise alone.

Other PCSK-9 inhibitors:

  • Alirocumab and Evolocumab: Used in familial hypercholesterolemia and cardiovascular disease to lower LDL-C. Administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks or once monthly. Offen combined with statins for enhanced LDL-C reduction.
  • Inclisiran: A newer agent that acts as a small interfering RNA (siRNA), reducing PCSK9 production.

Explanations of other options:

Ezetimibe (Option B): Ezetimibe lowers blood cholesterol by blocking the uptake of dietary and biliary cholesterol in the small intestine and is distinct from PCSK9 inhibitors.

Bempedoic acid (Option C): Bempedoic acid is a newer lipid-lowering drug that targets ATP-citrate lyase, an enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, and unlike PCSK9 inhibitors, it works through a different mechanism.

Clofibrate (Option D): Clofibrate, a fibrate drug, acts by stimulating peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), enhancing fatty acid breakdown and improving lipid levels, and it does not act on PCSK9.

question_text: 58-year-old woman with longstanding hypothyroidism was diagnosed with uterine fibroids and started on iron recently. Her other medications include levothyroxine, atorvastatin, and hydrochlorothiazide. A TSH is checked, and it is elevated to 15 mU/L. Which of the following is the most likely reason for her elevated TSH?
option_c: Poor absorption of levothyroxine due to ferrous sulfate
explanation:
• An increase in TSH in a patient with hypothyroidism that was previously stable with medication for many years suggests either a failure of taking the medication, difficulty with absorption from bowel disease, or medication interaction or drug– drug interaction affecting clearance.
  • In patients with normal body weight taking >200 μg of levothyroxine per day, an elevated TSH strongly suggests noncompliance. Such patients should be encouraged to take two tablets at one time on the day they remember to attempt to reach the weekly target dose; the long drug half-life makes this practice safe.
  • Other causes of increased thyroxine requirements include malabsorption, such as with celiac disease or small bowel surgery, estrogen therapy, and drugs that interfere with T4 absorption (e.g., ferrous sulfate, cholestyramine) or clearance (e.g., lovastatin, amiodarone, carbamazepine, phenytoin).

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg. no. 699

question_text: A  45-year-old man is also started on high-intensity atorvastatin therapy, along with antiplatelet therapy and appropriate medications to control blood pressure. Four weeks later, the patient's total cholesterol level is 140 mg/dL, down from 200 mg/dL before discharge. Which of the following has most likely increased as the result of the therapy?
explanation:
• HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins) inhibit the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis. In response to these changes, hepatocytes increase their surface expression of the LDL receptor to increase uptake of circulating LDL. Treatment generally produces a 20%-50% reduction in serum cholesterol and LDL concentration.
  • High-intensity statin therapy reduces the risk of acute coronary events. This risk reduction is greater than that seen with other classes of lipid- lowering medications and is likely due to additional properties of statins. Besides effects on lipids, statins have anti-inflammatory properties improve endothelial dysfunction, and appear to stabilize atherosclerotic plaques.

Reference:

Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 217

question_text:
Which of the following is true regarding bempedoic acid?
1. It is a non-competitive inhibitor of ATP-citrate lyase
2. It is a dicarboxylic acid
3. It inhibits de novo cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes
4. It can be used concomitantly with statins
explanation:
Explanation:

Bempedoic acid is chemically an α, omega-dicarboxylic acid (a fatty-acid-like molecule).

Mechanism: It is a prodrug that is activated in the liver to its CoA thioester; the active form Competitively inhibits ATP-citrate lyase (ACL) (Statement 1 ruled out) - an enzyme upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Thereby reducing de novo cholesterol synthesis in hepatocytes and lowering LDL-C.

Clinical use / combination: Bempedoic acid is indicated as an adjunct to statins (or for statin-intolerant patients) and can be combined with statins - but note important pharmacokinetic interactions (it can increase statin exposure modestly, especially simvastatin/pravastatin), so monitoring and dose adjustments may be needed.

question_text: A patient on hypertension was started in anti-hypertensive medications. Which of the following drugs would have caused this adverse effect?
explanation:
This is an image of angioedema, a side effects of ACE inhibitors like Captopril and Lisinopril.

Adverse effects

The adverse effect profile of all ACE inhibitors is similar.

  • Hypotension: an initial sharp fall in BP occurs especially in diuretic treated and CHF patients; persistent hypotension maybe troublesome in MI patients.
  • Hyperkalaemia: This is likely in patients with impaired renal function and in those taking K+ sparing diuretics, NSAIDs or β blockers.
  • Cough: a persistent brassy cough occurs in 10-16% patients within 1-8 weeks, appears to be caused by inhibition of bradykinin/substance P breakdown in the lungs of susceptible individuals.
  • Rashes, urticaria: occur in 1-4% recipients;
  • Dysgeusia: reversible loss or alteration of taste sensation due to captopril occurs in few patients, rarely with other ACE inhibitors.
  • Foetopathic: fetal growth retardation, hypoplasia of organs and fetal death may occur if ACE inhibitors are given during the later half of pregnancy.
  • Headache, dizziness, nausea and bowel upset:
  • Granulocytopenia and proteinuria: These are rare, but warrant withdrawal.
  • Acute renal failure: It may be precipitated by ACE inhibitors in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis due to fall in glomerular filtration pressure.
