question_text: Codeine, oxycodone and hydroxycodone undergo metabolism in liver by _________.
explanation:
• Hepatic oxidative metabolism is the primary route of degradation of the phenylpiperidine opioids (meperidine, fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil) and eventually leaves only small quantities of the parent compound unchanged for excretion. However, accumulation of a demethylated metabolite of meperidine, normeperidine, may occur in patients with decreased renal function and in those receiving multiple high doses of the drug.
  • In high concentrations, normeperidine may cause seizures. In contrast, no active metabolites of fentanyl have been reported. The P450 isozyme CYP3A4 metabolizes fentanyl by N -dealkylation in the liver.
  • CYP3A4 also present in the mucosa of the small intestine and contributes to the first-pass metabolism of fentanyl when it is taken orally. Codeine, oxycodone, and hydrocodone undergo metabolism in the liver by P450 isozyme CYP2D6, resulting in the production of metabolites of greater potency. For example, codeine is demethylated to morphine. Genetic polymorphism of CYP2D6 has been documented and linked to the variation in analgesic response seen among patients.

Reference: LANG’ Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 31- Opioid Analgesics & Antagonists by Dr. Mark A. Schumacher,PhD,MD, Dr. Alan I. Basbaum,PhD,& Dr. Walter L. Way,MD. Page no. 546

• Although fentanyl is now the predominant analgesic in the phenylpiperidine class, meperidine continues to be used. This older opioid has significant antimuscarinic effects, which may be a contraindication if tachycardia would be a problem.
  • Meperidine is also reported to have a negative inotropic action on the heart. In addition, it has the potential for producing seizures secondary to accumulation of its metabolite, normeperidine, in patients receiving high doses or with concurrent renal failure. Given this undesirable profile, use of meperidine as a first-line analgesic is becoming increasingly rare.

question_text: A 40-year-old woman comes to the office with a 4-week history of diarrhea accompanied by occasional abdominal bloating. explanation:
• This patient has uncomplicated diarrhea with benign findings on initial examination and evaluation. Common causes include irritable bowel syndrome and functional diarrhea. In such cases, empiric symptomatic therapy is often considered prior to more complex testing.
  • Diphenoxylate is an opioid anti-diarrheal agent structurally related to meperidine. It binds to mu opiate receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and slows motility. Low doses relieve diarrhea without other significant opiate effects. However, higher doses can produce morphine-like euphoria and physical dependence. question_text:
A 47-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics. She was found unconscious on a park bench by a bystander. Her history is unobtainable.
Vitals include a pulse of 64/min, a respiratory rate of 7/min, and a blood pressure of 90/70 mm Hg. On examination, the patient is unresponsive to voice and touch but shows a flexor response to pain. Her breathing is shallow. The pupils are constricted, and a response to light cannot be determined.
An arterial blood gas sample reveals:
pH - 7.26
PCO2 - 70 mmHg
HCO3 - 26mEq/L
explanation:
This patient's presentation is consistent with an opioid overdose and shows the typical triad of coma, respiratory depression, and miosis.

Furthermore, the arterial blood gas analysis shows a respiratory acidosis, which is expected due to decreased ventilation that results in carbon dioxide retention (elevated arterial Pco,) and decreased pH. Renal compensation then increases HCO, but this develops slowly, over at least 24 hours, and often the acute respiratory insult has resolved by then.

Opioids act directly on the respiratory center and can cause significant depression in overdose states. Another potential cause of acute respiratory acidosis is sudden airway obstruction which would trap exhaled air, including carbon dioxide, in the lungs. The graph below illustrates the ABG changes seen in respiratory acidosis and alkalosis.

Option A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients retain CO, over a prolonged period, and thus renal compensation (increased serum bicarbonate) compensates for the pulmonary acidosis. This patient, however, has an uncompensated respiratory acidosis more in line with an acute event (opioid overdose) than a chronic condition. Furthermore, an acute exacerbation of COPD would likely not render a person unconscious unless exceptionally severe.

Option B: Type 1 diabetics dependent upon insulin can develop diabetic ketoacidosis following non-compliance with medications and diet, infection, pregnancy, myocardial infarction, pancreatitis, and others. Diabetic ketoacidosis is a type of metabolic acidosis which would present with a decreased blood bicarbonate level and decreased carbon dioxide due to increased ventilation, which will blow off increasing quantities of the gas.

Option C: Most diuretics, like furosemide and thiazides, cause potassium and hydrogen ion wasting, leading to a contraction alkalosis. Since this patient presented with acidosis, diuretic abuse is unlikely.

Learning objective: Respiratory acidosis is characterized by an increased PCO2 and lowered pH. After compensation develops, the HCO3- concentration increases. Opioids are a known cause of respiratory depression that can cause respiratory acidosis.

Reference: Guyton & Hall, 14th edition pg no. 560, 561, 562

question_text: A 50 years old male patient came to emergency department with complaints of difficulty in breathing, bilateral lower limb oedema, chest pain. Sweating. Patient was on treatment for asthma but he did not take medications for 3,4 months. His SpO2 was 97% on air. explanation:
The relief produced by intravenous morphine in dyspnea from pulmonary edema associated with left ventricular heart failure is remarkable. Proposed mechanisms include reduced anxiety ( perception of shortness of breath) and reduced cardiac preload (reduced venous tone) and afterload (decreased peripheral resistance). However, if respiratory depression is a problem, furosemide may be preferred for the treatment of pulmonary edema. On the other hand, morphine can be particularly useful when treating painful myocardial ischemia with pulmonary edema.

Explanation:

question_text: Which are the pure opioid antagonist agents ?
explanation:
The pure opioid antagonist drugs naloxone, naltrexone, and nalmefene are morphine derivatives with bulkier substituents at the N 17 position. question_text: Which of the following is NOT an indication for a GnRH antagonist?
option_a: Prevent premature LH surge during controlled ovarian stimulation (IVF)
explanation:
Explanation:

GnRH antagonists (e.g., cetrorelix, ganirelix, and oral elagolix/relugolix in some uses; degarelix is used in prostate cancer) suppress gonadotropin release promptly by blocking GnRH receptors- leading to reduced LH/FSH and sex steroid production.
Indications include:

  • Prevention of premature LH surge (Option A) during controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (short course antagonists are widely used in IVF cycles).
  • Advanced prostate cancer (Option C): GnRH antagonists (degarelix) lower testosterone quickly without initial flare seen with agonists.
  • Endometriosis / uterine fibroids (Option D): GnRH analogues (agonists and some antagonists like elagolix) are used to suppress estrogen production and reduce disease activity.

Hypogonadism is a condition of low sex steroids - treating it requires replacement (testosterone or estrogen), not further suppression. Thus GnRH antagonists (which suppress gonadal function) are contraindicated for treating hypogonadism.

Key takeaways:

GnRH antagonists = agents to suppress gonadal steroid production - used when suppression is desired (IVF control, prostate cancer, endometriosis), never to treat hypogonadism.

question_text: A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department with difficulty breathing and cyanosis after being exposed to carbon monoxide gas in a garage while repairing a vehicle. Despite receiving 100% oxygen, his oxygen saturation remains low and does not improve. What type of hypoxia is most likely responsible for his symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

Due to low oxygen carrying capacity of blood. Eg: Massive haemorrhage, Carbon Monoxide poisoning.

Carbon Monoxide (CO) has an affinity for haemoglobin which is 230-270 times greater than that of oxygen. Thus, in spite of adequate partial pressure of oxygen in blood, there is reduced arterial oxygen content. CO causes a leftward shift of oxygen dissociation curve, thus affecting the offloading of oxygen from haemoglobin to the tissues. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy is considered to be the antidote in CO poisoning.

Explanation of other options:

Histotoxic (Option A): Histotoxic - Tissues cannot utilise oxygen. Eg: Cyanide poisoning

Stagnant (Option B): Stagnant - Due to impaired circulation. Egs: Cardiac failure, Shock

Hypoxic (Option D): Hypoxic - due to reduced oxygen in the atmosphere or mechanical obstruction.

Key Takeaways:

Gordon's classification of Anoxia - Anaemic, Hypoxic, Stagnant and Histotoxic.

CO gas is usually emitted from vehicle exhaust and it can cause Anaemic Anoxia. CO) has an affinity for haemoglobin which is 230-270 times greater than that of oxygen. It results in decreased ability of oxygen to be carried by the blood and released to the tissues. Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy is considered to be the antidote in CO poisoning.

question_text: How should the steroid therapy be administered for a 55-year-old male diagnosed with Addison’s disease?
option_b: Bolus of 100mg followed by 200mg over 24 hours
option_c: Bolus of 200 mg followed by 500 mg over 24 hours
explanation:
Explanation:

In a 55-year-old man with Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency), steroid therapy is usually started with a 100 mg bolus dose which is followed by 200 mg given over the subsequent 24 hours.

  • Hydrocortisone, a synthetic glucocorticoid with both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity, is the preferred treatment for acute adrenal insufficiency.
  • It replaces deficient cortisol and helps maintain physiological balance.
  • The usual dosage is 10-12 mg/m²/day, beginning with a 100 mg bolus, followed by 200 mg administered over 24 hours.
  • The purpose of the initial 100 mg bolus is to rapidly raise cortisol levels and address the acute deficiency.
  • The subsequent 200 mg infusion over 24 hours provides a steady supply of cortisol, ensuring stable levels and continuous hormonal coverage throughout the day.

question_text: A patient diagnosed with schizophrenia has been on olanzapine therapy for a few months. Although the drug effectively controlled the symptoms, the patient discontinued the medication. What is the most likely reason for discontinuation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Olanzapine

  • This antipsychotic; resembles clozapine in blocking multiple monoaminergic (D2, 5-HT2, α1, α2) as well as muscarinic and H1 receptors.
  • Both positive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia are improved.
  • A broader spectrum of efficacy covering schizo-affective disorders has been demonstrated, and it is approved for use in mania.
  • Olanzapine is a potent antimuscarinic, produces dry mouth and constipation.
  • Weaker D2 blockade results in few extrapyramidal side effects and little rise in prolactin levels, but is more epileptogenic than high potency phenothiazines.
  • It causes weight gain and carries a higher risk of impairing glucose tolerance or worsening diabetes as well as elevating serum triglyceride. These metabolic complications have discouraged its use.

Explanation of other options:

Tardive Dyskinesia (Option A):

  • Tardive dyskinesia is a potential side effect of long-term antipsychotic use, but it is more commonly associated with first-generation antipsychotics rather than second-generation drugs like olanzapine.
  • Tardive dyskinesia is less common with olanzapine, and while it may occur, it is unlikely to be the primary reason for discontinuation.

Agranulocytosis (Option C):

  • Agranulocytosis is a rare but serious side effect of clozapine, not olanzapine.
  • It is not commonly associated with olanzapine therapy and is not the most likely reason for discontinuation.

Muscular dystonia (Option D):

  • Muscular dystonia (or dystonic reactions) is more often seen with first-generation antipsychotics that cause extrapyramidal side effects.
  • Although olanzapine may cause mild extrapyramidal symptoms, these are generally less severe than with first-generation antipsychotics and are unlikely to be the main reason for discontinuation.

Key Takeaways:

Olanzapine causes weight gain and carries a higher risk of impairing glucose tolerance or worsening diabetes as well as elevating serum triglyceride. These metabolic complications have discouraged its use.

question_text: A patient is initiated on the 3HP regimen (Isoniazid + Rifapentine once weekly for 3 months) for tuberculosis preventive therapy (TPT). Which of the following statements about the 3HP regimen is true?
option_a: There is more compliance in 3HP than in 9H and 6H.
option_b: There is no significant difference in compliance between 3HP, 6H, and 9H.
option_c: The chance of abortion in 3HP is the same as in 6H.
option_d: The 3HP regimen is less effective than 6H and 9H in preventing active tuberculosis.
explanation:
Explanation:

The 3HP regimen, consisting of a 3-month course of weekly rifapentine and isoniazid, offers higher patient compliance compared to the longer 9H (9-month isoniazid) and 6H (6-month isoniazid) regimens. Its shorter duration improves adherence and minimises the risk of treatment interruptions, enhancing overall effectiveness.

Tuberculosis Prevention Therapy (TPT): Treatment given to individuals who are at high risk of developing active TB & prevent progression from latent TB infection.

TB prophylaxis is indicated in the following high-risk patient groups:

  • Contacts of open cases who show recent Mantoux conversion.
  • Children with a sputum-positive TB patient in the family.
  • Neonate of a tubercular mother.
  • Patients with leukaemia, diabetes, silicosis or those receiving immunosuppressant medication or those on long-term corticosteroid therapy.
  • HIV-infected contacts of sputum-positive cases.

The recommended regimens for tuberculosis treatment include the following options:

  • 6H or 9H: Isoniazid (5 mg/kg) daily for 6 months (6H) or 9 months (9H).
  • 3HP: Rifapentine (10 mg/kg) combined with high-dose Isonazid (15 mg/kg) weekly for 3 months.
  • 4R: Rifampin (10 mg/kg) daily for 4 months.
  • 3HR: Isoniazid (5 mg/kg) and Rifampin (10 mg/kg) daily for 3 months. 

The chance of abortion in 3HP is the same as in 6H (Option C): The difference in the duration of exposure leads to a different side effect profile, and the risk of pregnancy-related complications, including abortion, is not the same in both regimens. 

The 3HP regimen is less effective than 6H and 9H in preventing active tuberculosis (Option D): It is incorrect because 3HP is as effective, if not slightly more effective, in preventing active TB when compared to the longer regimens of 6H and 9H. 

Reference:

  1. https://www.cdc.gov/tb/topic/treatment/ltbi.htm#:~:text=CDC%20and%20the%20National%20Tuberculosis,weekly%20isoniazid%20plus%20rifapentine%20(3HP)

question_text: A patient with a pituitary tumor secreting excess growth hormone had surgery, but the tumor could not be completely excised. What is the preferred first-line therapy in this situation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Octreotide is the first-line therapy for patients with growth hormone-secreting pituitary tumors when surgical removal is incomplete.

  • Octreotide, a synthetic analogue of somatostatin, suppresses growth hormone (GH) release from the pituitary and can be administered intravenously or subcutaneously, with a longer-lasting effect than natural somatostatin.
  • Medical management is the choice when curative surgery is not possible or when GH levels remain elevated after resection.

Explanations of other options:

Leuprolide (Option A): Leuprolide, a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, suppresses the secretion of LH and FSH and is mainly used in treating prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids, and precocious puberty.

Goserelin (Option B): Goserelin, a GnRH agonist like leuprolide, is mainly utilized for managing prostate cancer, breast cancer, and endometriosis.

Nafarelin (Option C): Nafarelin is a GnRH agonist mainly prescribed for the management of endometriosis and precocious puberty.

question_text: What is the most significant adverse effect associated with long-term tamoxifen therapy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist in breast tissue but as a partial agonist in the endometrium. This agonist effect can stimulate endometrial proliferation, leading to endometrial hyperplasia, polyps, and an increased risk of endometrial cancer, which is its most significant long-term adverse effect.

Explanation of other options:

Cancer in the opposite breast (Option A): Tamoxifen reduces the risk of contralateral breast cancer.

Osteoporosis (Option B): Tamoxifen has an estrogen-agonistic effect on bone, helping to preserve bone density in postmenopausal women, not cause osteoporosis.

Infertility (Option D): While it can cause menstrual irregularities, this is not its most significant defined risk.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tamoxifen has tissue-specific effects: antagonist in breast, agonist in endometrium and bone.
  • Patients on tamoxifen require regular gynecological monitoring.

question_text: A male patient with COPD was started on theophylline therapy. By the next day, he observed an increase in urine output. Through which receptor is this effect of the drug mediated?
explanation:
Explanation:

The rise in urine output seen in this patient on theophylline occurs due to its action on adenosine A1 receptors.

  • Theophylline acts as a nonselective antagonist at adenosine receptors, blocking adenosine activity at A1, A2A, A2B, and A3 subtypes.
  • Its inhibition of renal A1 receptors specifically results in enhanced glomerular filtration and promotes diuresis.

Explanations of other options:

Interleukin-10 (Option A): Interleukin-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that helps control immune activity by preventing excessive inflammatory injury. It does not play a direct role in producing diuresis or in the pharmacological actions of theophylline.

Histone deacetylase (Option B): Histone deacetylases are enzymes that influence gene regulation by stripping acetyl groups from histone proteins. They do not contribute to the diuretic action of theophylline.

Beta 2 adrenergic receptors (Option D): Beta-2 adrenergic receptors are mainly located in the lungs, where their stimulation leads to bronchodilation. They are absent in the kidneys.

Key takeaway:

Adenosine A1 receptors are present in the kidneys and play a role in controlling fluid and electrolyte homeostasis. Inhibition of these receptors by theophylline results in enhanced urine output and diuresis.

question_text: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is already on inhaled salmeterol therapy, but they are currently experiencing no improvement and have presented to the outpatient department. Which of the following medications can be included in their treatment plan?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ipratropium bromide is a muscarinic (M3) receptor antagonist that provides bronchodilation by inhibiting parasympathetic-mediated bronchoconstriction. It is especially effective in COPD patients with structurally narrowed airways.

Mechanism of Action:

  • Blocks M3 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle → prevents acetylcholine-induced bronchoconstriction → bronchodilation.
  • Acts primarily on larger airways.
  • Minimal effect in normal airways; significant effect in COPD due to increased airway resistance.
  • The bronchodilation effect is minimal in normal airways.
  • The effect is more significant in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patients.
  • COPD patients have structurally narrowed airways.
  • Higher airway resistance in COPD is due to the inverse relationship between airway resistance and the fourth power of the airway radius.

question_text:
Which of the following sentences are TRUE for use of artemisinin-based combination therapy in pregnancy?
1. Recommended for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in 2nd & 3rd trimester
2. Not recommended for uncomplicated falciparum malaria in 2nd & 3rd trimester
3. Intravenous artesunate can be used for severe malaria in 1st trimester
4. Intravenous artesunate cannot be used for severe malaria in 1st trimester
explanation:
WHO recommends:

  • Artemisinin-based combination therapies for the treatment of uncomplicated falciparum malaria during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy.
  • Intravenous artesunate or quinine for the treatment of severe malaria during the first trimester.
  • And intravenous artesunate for treatment of severe malaria during the second and third trimesters.

Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 921

question_text: Which of the following is the first-line treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The recommended treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria is Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy (ACT).
  • For severe or complicated cases, current guidelines recommend intravenous artesunate as the first-line treatment. It is highly effective in rapidly reducing parasite load and has been shown to significantly lower mortality in severe malaria.
  • While drugs like quinine and artemether are also effective, artesunate is preferred due to its faster action and greater efficacy.
  • Chloroquine is not recommended for P. falciparum malaria because the parasite has developed widespread resistance, making the drug ineffective in most cases. (Option A ruled out)

Complicated malaria, a life-threatening condition caused by P. falciparum, requires parenteral treatment:

  • First-line: IV artesunate (preferred)
  • Second-line: IM artemether or arteether
  • Third-line: IV quinine in 5% dextrose (caution: quinine may cause hypoglycemia)

Explanation for other options:

Primaquine (Option B): interferes with the parasite's electron transport chain and is primarily used for the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale by targeting dormant liver stages (hypnozoites). It is not used to treat P. falciparum malaria.

Doxycycline (Option C): is commonly used for malaria prophylaxis or as an add-on in combination therapy, but it is not the preferred first-line treatment for Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

question_text: Which of the following sentence is FALSE for Artemisinin?
option_a: Artemisinin is available for intravenous use
option_b: They are very rapidly acting blood schizonticides
option_c: They have no effect on hepatic stage
explanation:
• The artemisinin is now widely available around the world.
  • However, artemisinin monotherapy for the treatment of uncomplicated malaria is now strongly discouraged. Rather, co-formulated artemisinin-based combination therapies are recommended to improve efficacy and prevent the selection of artemisinin-resistant parasites.
  • The oral combination regimen Coartem (artemether lumefantrine) was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2009, and may be considered the new first-line therapy in the USA for uncomplicated falciparum malaria, although the drug may not be widely available.
  • Intravenous artesunate was made available by the CDC in 2007; use of the drug can be initiated
  • by contact with the CDC, which will release the drug for appropriate indications (falciparum malaria with signs of severe disease or inability to take oral medications) from stocks stored around the USA.
  • Artemisinin and its analogs are very rapidly acting blood schizonticides against all human malaria parasites. Artemisinin has no effect on hepatic stages.
  • The antimalarial activity of artemisinin may result from the production of free radicals that follows the iron-catalysed cleavage of the artemisinin endoperoxide bridge in the parasite food vacuole or from inhibition of a parasite calcium ATPase.
  • Artemisinin resistance is not yet an important problem, but P falciparum isolates with diminished in vitro susceptibility to artemether have recently been described.
  • In addition, increasing rates of treatment failure and increases in parasite clearance times after use
  • of artesunate or artesunate-mefloquine in parts of Cambodia may be early signs of a worrisome decrease in artesunate efficacy.

Reference: LANG' Basic & clinical pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung, Susen B. Masters and Anthony J. Trevor 12th edition. Chapter 52- Antiprotozoal Agents by Dr. Philip J. Rosenthal, MD. Page no. 920

question_text: A pregnant woman in the first trimester presents with complicated malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum resistant to chloroquine. Which of the following is the treatment of choice?
explanation:
Explanation:

Complicated or severe malaria is defined by the presence of life-threatening manifestations, which may include:

  • Cerebral malaria:Altered consciousness, seizures.
  • Severe anemia:Hemoglobin <5 g/dL.
  • Acute renal failure:Oliguria, elevated creatinine.
  • Hypoglycemia, shock, pulmonary edema, or severe parasitemia.

In pregnancy, malaria carries additional maternal and fetal risks such as miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm labor, and low birth weight. Thus, prompt and effective therapy is critical.

Artesunate is the preferred first-line therapy for complicated P. falciparum malaria, regardless of the trimester.

Artesunate:

1. Mechanism of Action:

  1. Artesunate is an artemisinin derivativethat generates free radicals in the parasite-infected red blood cells, causing rapid parasite death.
  2. It has rapid onset of actionand is highly effective in clearing parasitemia.

2. Safety in Pregnancy:

  1. Although initial animal studies suggested potential teratogenicity, extensive clinical data and WHO guidelines now support its use even in the first trimesterfor severe malaria.
  2. The risk of maternal and fetal death from severe malaria far outweighs theoretical drug risks.

3. Advantages Over Quinine:

  1. Faster parasite clearance, improved maternal survival, fewer side effects.
  2. Quinine is associated with cinchonism(tinnitus, headache, nausea, visual disturbances) and hypoglycemia, which can complicate pregnancy management.
  3. Quinine is still used as first-line therapy for uncomplicated malaria in the first trimester, often combined with Clindamycin.

4. Administration:

  1. Intravenous Artesunateis given as 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, and 24 hours, then daily until the patient can tolerate oral therapy.
  2. Transition to an oral ACT(artemether-lumefantrine) may follow once the patient stabilizes.

Explanation of Other Options:

Quinine (Option A):

  • Effective for uncomplicated malaria in early pregnancy but inferior to IV Artesunatefor severe malaria.
  • Associated with cinchonism, hypoglycemia, and requires longer treatment duration.
  • May be considered second-lineif Artesunate is unavailable.

Sulfadoxine/Pyrimethamine (Option B):

  • Contraindicated in first trimesterbecause pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist, increasing the risk of neural tube defects.
  • Used for intermittent preventive therapyonly in the second and third trimesters, not for active infection.

Primaquine (Option D):

  • Targets hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale, not P. falciparum.
  • Absolutely contraindicated in pregnancydue to the risk of hemolysis in G6PD-deficient fetuses, for whom testing is not feasible in utero.

question_text: A 30-year-old man recently returned from Assam presents with high-grade fever, chills, seizures, hypotension (BP 70/50 mmHg), and laboured breathing. Peripheral blood smear confirms Plasmodium falciparum infection. Which of the following is the drug of choice in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient has severe falciparum malaria with complications:
    • Cerebral involvement: seizures, altered sensorium
    • Hemodynamic compromise: hypotension
    • Respiratory distress: laboured breathing
  • Intravenous artesunate is the first-line therapy for severe malaria according to WHO and NVBDCP guidelines.
    • Rapid parasitic clearance
    • Safe in most populations, including pregnant women in 2nd/3rd trimester
    • Shortens duration of complications and reduces mortality

Complicated malaria is a life-threatening form of malaria caused by P. falciparum. Treatment is given parenterally.

  • DOC: IV Artemisinin
  • 2nd: IM artemether/arteether
  • 3rd: IV Quinine in 5% dextrose (quinine is hypoglycemic)

Explanation of Other Options

Chloroquine (Option A):

  • Effective for uncomplicated P. vivax malaria in areas without resistance
  • Ineffective in chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum, which is widespread in Assam
  • Not suitable for severe malaria

Quinine (Option B):

  • IV quinine is a second-line therapy for severe malaria
  • Slower onset than artesunate, risk of hypoglycemia and cardiac toxicity
  • Used if artesunate is unavailable

Artemether (Option D):

  • Used IM for severe malaria, especially in resource-limited settings
  • IV artesunate preferred due to faster parasitic clearance and higher efficacy

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Severe falciparum malaria is life-threatening → requires parenteral therapy.
  • IV artesunate: preferred first-line due to rapid parasite clearance and reduced mortality.
  • Quinine: second-line; monitor cardiac and glucose levels.
  • Chloroquine: not recommended in chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum areas.
  • Artemisinin derivatives: rapid action, suitable for both severe and uncomplicated malaria in combination therapy.
  • Recognize signs of severe malaria: cerebral involvement, hypotension, acidosis, renal failure, respiratory distress.

question_text: Mechanism of action of botulinum toxin is?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mechanism of Action:

  • Botulinum toxin inhibits the exocytosis of acetylcholine (ACh) at cholinergic nerve terminals.
  • It acts by interfering with SNARE proteins involved in vesicle fusion at the neuromuscular junction.
  • This results in a long-lasting blockade of cholinergic transmission, leading to flaccid paralysis of affected muscles.

Source:

  • Produced by Clostridium botulinum.
  • Botulinum toxin types A and B are most commonly used clinically.
  • Responsible for the clinical condition botulism, a form of food poisoning.

Adverse Effects (Anticholinergic-like):

  • Dry mouth
  • Blurred vision
  • Constipation
  • Urinary retention

Therapeutic Uses of Botulinum Toxin A (BOTOX):

Neurological and Spastic Disorders:

  • Blepharospasm
  • Spastic cerebral palsy
  • Strabismus
  • Spasmodic torticollis
  • Nystagmus
  • Hemifacial spasm
  • Post-stroke spasticity
  • Spasmodic dysphonia
  • Prophylaxis of chronic migraine
  • Axillary hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating)
  • Cosmetic use for wrinkles (facial lines)

Explanation of other option:

Block postsynaptic receptors of acetylcholine

  • Botulinum toxin does not block postsynaptic receptors of acetylcholine.
  • It acts presynaptically to inhibit the release of acetylcholine, rather than interfering with the receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

Inhibit reuptake of acetylcholine

  • Botulinum toxin does not act by inhibiting the reuptake of acetylcholine.
  • Its action is focused on preventing acetylcholine release, not on reuptake.

Inhibit acetylcholine esterase

  • Botulinum toxin does not affect acetylcholinesterase activiy.
  • Acetylcholinesterase is responsible for breaking down acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, but botulinum toxin's mechanism is unrelated to this enzyme.

Key Takeaways:

Botulinum toxin acts by inhibiting the exocytosis of ACh.

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with urinary hesitancy and retention. Ultrasound reveals a post-void residual urine volume of 130 ml. Which medication would provide the most immediate symptom relief ?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario with features of urinary retention and hesitancy is suggestive of BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) and alpha-1 blockers can provide immediate symptom relief.


Explanation of other options:

Calcium channel blockers (Option A): Mainly prescribed for managing hypertension, angina, and some cardiac arrhythmias. They have no direct role in relieving urinary hesitancy or retention and are therefore not suitable for this patient's condition.

ACE inhibitors (Option C): Mainly prescribed for managing hypertension and heart failure. They do not specifically address urinary hesitancy or retention related to prostate enlargement.

Aldosterone antagonists (Option D): Commonly used in the management of heart failure, hypertension, and some kidney disorders by regulating fluid and electrolyte balance. They are not suitable for treating urinary hesitancy or retention due to prostate enlargement.

question_text: A female patient presents with burning during urination and other symptoms of a UTI. Which of the following fluoroquinolones is least effective against Enterococcus species in this infection?
explanation:
Explanation:

Moxifloxacin is less effective for treating urinary tract infections caused by Enterococcus species. Although it is a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone, its activity against Enterococcus is limited.

Ofloxacin (Option A): Ofloxacin achieves high urinary concentrations and exhibits good activity against Enterococcus and other common urinary pathogens. Therefore, it is effective in the treatment of urinary tract infections (UTIs).

Ciprofloxacin (Option B): Ciprofloxacin is a potent fluoroquinolone with broad-spectrum antibacterial activity. It is particularly effective against Gram-negative organisms and is commonly used in UTIs. It also exhibits moderate activity against Enterococcus species.

Levofloxacin (Option D): Levofloxacin is the L-isomer of ofloxacin and has enhanced potency against Gram-positive organisms, including Enterococcus species. It also achieves excellent urinary excretion, making it a suitable choice for UTI management.

question_text: A female patient with symptoms of urinary tract infection was prescribed an antibiotic that later led to tendon rupture and joint problems. What is the drug’s mechanism of action?
explanation:
Explanation:

The drug described is a fluoroquinolone, a class of antibiotics commonly used for UTIs, respiratory tract infections, and several systemic bacterial infections.

  • A well-recognised adverse effect of fluoroquinolones is tendon rupture and arthropathy, particularly in older individuals and those on corticosteroids.
  • Examples: Ciprofloxacin, Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin.

Mechanism of Action of Fluoroquinolones:


Adverse Effects of Fluoroquinolones:

  • Gastrointestinal upset (nausea, diarrhoea)
  • CNS manifestations (headache, dizziness)
  • Tendonitis and tendon rupture
  • QT prolongation
  • Photosensitivity
  • May worsen myasthenia gravis

Exclusion of Other Options:

Ribosomal inhibition (Option B): Seen with macrolides, tetracyclines, and aminoglycosides; not linked to tendon injury.

Cell wall synthesis inhibition (Option C): Penicillins and cephalosporins inhibit bacterial cell wall formation, but do not cause tendon rupture.

Folic acid synthesis inhibition (Option D): Sulfonamides and trimethoprim act here, with no association with arthropathy.

question_text: A 32-year-old woman complaints of burning upon urination. Urinalysis shows 1+ WBC/hpf, 1+ RBC/hpf, and abundant bacteria, with mostly gram-negative rods. Treatment is begun with a drug that is associated with the development of tendon rupture. This drug most likely interferes with which of the following processes?
option_d: Insertion of negative supercoils in DNA
explanation:
• Urinary tract infections in adults are primarily associated with dysuria with accompanying urinary urgency and frequency. There may be a sensation of bladder fullness or lower abdominal discomfort. Treatment includes the use of fluoroquinolones, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX), nitrofurantoin, or cephalosporins. Some patients may also require a urinary analgesic such as oral phenazopyridine, which is useful to relieve discomfort due to severe dysuria.
  • In this question, you must determine which UTI treatment option is associated with the development of tendon rupture. Commonly used bactericidal fluoroquinolones include ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, and ofloxacin, among others. These antibiotics act by inhibiting DNA gyrase. Topoisomerases such as DNA gyrase (DNA topoisomerase Il) can insert negative supercoils to relieve the positive supercoiling that occurs as the replication fork proceeds down the length of the chromosome. The fluoroquinolones are associated with the development of tendon rupture and arthropathy in younger children under the age of 18 years as well as phototoxicity, CNS stimulation, and a variety of Gl side effects. The fluoroquinolones are classified as pregnancy category C agents.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 836

question_text: A 14-day-old infant is brought because of decreased alertness and poor feeding. Laboratory studies show an unconjugated bilirubin level of 33 mg/dL. Which of the following drugs taken by the mother during the third trimester is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
explanation:
• Jaundice is a common condition seen in newborns that requires medical attention. As a result of an accumulation of unconjugated bilirubin, there may be a yellow coloration of the skin and sclera in newborns with jaundice. Neonatal jaundice can result from increased breakdown of fetal erythrocytes coupled with low hepatic excretory capacity.
  • Thus high levels of unconjugated bilirubin (a breakdown product of hemoglobin) causes can cause jaundice and even kernicterus, which is a complication of neonatal jaundice. Kernicterus is the chronic and permanent neuroloqic sequelae of bilirubin-induced neurologic dysfunction (BIND). Brain regions most commonly affected include the basal ganglia and brainstem nuclei involved in oculomotor and auditory function.
  • Acute hyperbilirubinemia can lead to decreased alertness, hypotonia and poor feeding. Kernicterus is associated with opisthotonos, a high-pitched cry, an abnormal Moro reflex, and abnormal eye movements. Although kernicterus can occur pathologically, this condition may also occur if the mother takes sulfonamide antibiotics, such as trimethoprim- sulfamethoxazole or sulfisoxazole during the 2nd or 3rd trimester of pregnancy. Sulfonamides can displace bilirubin from itsalbumin-binding site, thereby increasing the serum concentration of free bilirubin available to cross the blood-brain barrier.
  • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is not recommended for use in infants less than 2 months old. When hyperbilirubinemia occurs in an infant, the treatment of choice is to remove the bilirubin from the blood by phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 817

question_text: A 46-year-old man comes with fever, perianal pain, and dysuria. Rectal examination shows a boggy, tender prostate. Gram stain of the urine shows gram-negative rods. He is given an oral antibiotic and returns three weeks later complaining of fatigue and shortness of breath. A complete blood count shows a hemoglobin of 12 g/dL and a blood smear stained with methylene blue shows small blue granules located near the periphery of some of the erythrocytes. With which of the following antibiotics was the patient most likely treated?
explanation:
• This patient has acute prostatitis, which is characterized by fever, chills, and dysuria, with a swollen, extremely tender prostate on rectal exam (this helps distinguish prostatitis from a simple urinary tract infection, which typically presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, and urinary urgency).
  • The urine Gram stain and culture will generally be positive. The most common pathogens in older men are gram-negatives such as Escherichia coli, Enterobacter, Serratia, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, and Proteus species. Urinary tract symptoms in young sexually active males may be caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis.
  • The treatment regimen for this bacterial infection is typically a 21-day course of ampicillin, a fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), or trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).
  • However, this patient also has symptoms and signs of G6PD deficiency, which is an X-linked recessive disorder. The blood smear describes Heinz bodies in the red cells, which are small aggregates of denatured hemoglobin that can appear in G6PD deficiency-related anemia.
  • The medications that commonly induce hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficient patients are sulfonamides (TMP-SMX), nitrofurantoin, dapsone, primaquine, and quinine. Fava beans can also have the same effect.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 834

question_text: A patient with schizophrenia developed muscular dystonia and was given treatment for it. He now presents with dry mouth, mydriasis, and urinary retention. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for these new symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Acute dystoniais a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotic drugs like haloperidol.
  • First-line treatment for dystonia is an anticholinergic agentsuch as benztropine or trihexyphenidyl.
  • Benztropine, by blocking muscarinic receptors, improves EPS but frequently produces anticholinergic side effectssuch as:
    • Dry mouth
    • Mydriasis (dilated pupils)
    • Urinary retention
    • Constipation
    • Blurred vision

Explanation of Other Options:

Haloperidol (Option A):

  • Haloperidol is a typical antipsychoticthat can cause acute dystonia due to potent dopamine D2 blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway.
  • It is not responsiblefor anticholinergic symptoms like dry mouth or urinary retention.

Quetiapine (Option B):

  • An atypical antipsychoticwith minimal EPS risk due to weak D2 blockade.
  • While it can cause sedation and metabolic effects, it does not produce the acute anticholinergic triadseen here.

Clozapine (Option D):

  • Another atypical antipsychotic, primarily associated with agranulocytosis, seizures, myocarditis, and metabolic syndrome.
  • It may cause mild anticholinergic effects, but the clinical setting here clearly implicates the anticholinergic given for dystonia(benztropine), not clozapine.

question_text: A female patient presents with burning during urination and is diagnosed with cystitis. Which of the following medications is appropriate for treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) is an antibiotic commonly used as the first-line treatment for uncomplicated cystitis.

Explanation for other options:

Amoxicillin (Option A): It is effective against various bacterial infections but is not the preferred choice for uncomplicated cystitis. Due to rising antibiotic resistance, it is rarely used as a first-line treatment.

Ciprofloxacin (Option B): It is a fluoroquinolone, is typically reserved for more complicated or resistant infections and is generally not recommended as first-line therapy for uncomplicated cystitis because of concerns about growing resistance.

Doxycycline (Option D): It is not commonly used to treat cystitis; it is more frequently prescribed for atypical infections like those caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Mycoplasma.

question_text: A 78-year-old man presents with headache and nonproductive cough for 5 days.  Results of cold agglutinin titer testing show a 4-fold elevation above normal. CXR shows diffuse, patchy infiltrates bilaterally. Treatment with an antibiotic acts by?
option_a: Free radical creation within bacterial cells
option_b: Inhibition of peptide translocation at the 50S ribosomal subunit
explanation:
• As per given clinical scenario this man has Mycoplasma pneumonia, which typically manifests with insidious onset and causes headaches and a nonproductive cough with diffuse, patchy infiltrates on chest x-ray. Erythrocyte agglutination is seen as a result of high titers of IgM cold agglutinins.
  • Macrolides such as erythromycin and azithromycin are often used to treat Mycoplasma pneumonia. These antibiotics inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S ribosomal RNA of the 50S subunit. Doxycycline (which inhibits protein synthesis by binding to the 30S subunit) and fluoroquinolones (which inhibit prokaryotic topoisomerases) are also effective against Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
  • Option A. Nitroimidazoles create free radicals within bacteria cells, which leads to DNA strand breaks, used to treat infections with anaerobic bacteria. They are not used to treat Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
  • Sulfonamides inhibit bacterial synthesis of folic acid by DHPS. Sulfamethoxazole is used in combination with trimethoprim (TMP-SMX) to treat Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (In immunocompromised). Sulfonamides are not indicated for Mycoplasma pneumoniae
  • Rifamycins inhibit bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, used to treat mycobacterial It is not used to treat Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

question_text: Which of the following is the preferred drug for treating a urinary tract infection (UTI) during pregnancy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ceftriaxone is the drug of choice for treating UTIs during pregnancy because it is effective against common causative organisms, such as Escherichia coli.

As a broad-spectrum antibiotic, it is generally considered safe for use in pregnant women.

Explanation of Other Options:

Amoxicillin (Option A): It is an antibiotic frequently used for gram-positive infections; however, it is less commonly chosen for UTIs due to increasing bacterial resistance.

Azithromycin (Option B): It is a macrolide antibiotic, is mainly used for respiratory tract infections and is not considered a first-line treatment for UTIs.

Clarithromycin (Option C): It is also primarily prescribed for respiratory infections and is generally not recommended as a first-line option for UTIs, as it may be less effective against the typical bacteria responsible for these infections.

question_text: A 56-year-old man is brought because of fever, chills, and productive cough for the past 4 days. Physical examination shows dullness to percussion, and decreased breath sounds are heard over the left lung base on auscultation of the chest. Gram stain of sputum shows abundant neutrophils and gram-positive diplococci. His past medical history is unremarkable. Which of the following drugs is most appropriate in the treatment of this patient?
explanation:
• Streptococcus pneumonia (pneumococcus) is classified as a gram-positive diplococcus. It is the most likely organism causing this man's pneumonia, based on the clinical presentation as well as the Gram stain results. Since the recommended empiric antibiotic regimen is different for community acquired pneumonia (CAP) in adults being treated in the outpatient vs. inpatient setting you must first determine if the patient requires hospital admission. Criteria for hospital admission are based on the clinical presentation of the patient. CURB-65 prognostic variables for hospitalisation is outlined below:
    • Confusion (based upon a specific mental test or disorientation to person, place, or time)
    • Urea (blood urea nitrogen in the United States) >7 mmol/L (20 mg/dL)
    • Respiratory rate >30 breaths/minute
    • Blood pressure [BP] (systolic <90 mmHg or diastolic <60 mrHg)
    • Age >65 years
  • In this case, the patient can be treated as an outpatient since he does not meet the criteria for admission. Current treatment guidelines for community acquired pneumonia established by the Infectious Disease Society of America and the American Thoracic Society (IDSA/ATS) mainly rely on macrolides (with or without a beta-lactam) or newer fluoroquinolones for outpatient therapy. The recommendations are as follows:
    • In previously healthy patients (such as the patient in this vignette) and no use of antimicrobials in the past three months the drugs of choice are a macrolide (azithromycin, clarithromycin or erythromycin) OR doxycycline.
    • If the patient has an established comorbidity (such as chronic, heart, lung, liver or renal disease, diabetes, or others), the use of a fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin, gemifloxacin, or levofloxacin) OR a beta-lactam (such as amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefuroxime or ceftriaxone) PLUS a macrolide is recommended.

In utero exposure can lead to discoloration of deciduous teeth and inhibition of bone growth, as seen in this patient. For this reason, tetracyclines are contraindicated during pregnancy and in children < 8 years of age.

question_text: What is the mechanism of action of doxycycline?
explanation:
Explanation:

Doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic, inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing the addition of amino acids to the growing peptide chain, thereby halting bacterial growth.

question_text: What dose adjustment is necessary for a patient who has initiated anti-tubercular therapy and is already receiving antiretroviral treatment with Tenofovir 200 mg, Dolutegravir 100 mg at night, and Lamivudine 200 mg?
option_a: Add tenofovir 200 mg in the morning
option_b: Add dolutegravir 100 mg in the morning
option_d: Add lamivudine 200 mg in the morning
explanation:
Explanation:
In this patient, the dose of Dolutegravir (an integrase inhibitor) needs to be increased. This is because Rifampicin, a key anti-tubercular drug, is a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes, which accelerates the metabolism of Dolutegravir, thereby reducing its plasma concentration and effectiveness.

Since Rifampicin significantly enhances drug metabolism via the CYP450 pathway, Dolutegravir levels may become subtherapeutic unless its dose is adjusted accordingly.

Explanation for other options:

Add Tenofovir 200 mg in the morning (Option A): Tenofovir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that is not significantly metabolized by the CYP450 enzyme system. Therefore, Rifampicin's enzyme-inducing effect does not affect Tenofovir's efficacy or safety, and no dose adjustment is needed.

No dose adjustment (Option C): This option is incorrect because Dolutegravir requires a dose increase due to Rifampicin's induction of its metabolism.

Add Lamivudine 200 mg in the morning (Option D): Like Tenofovir, Lamivudine is an NRTI and does not undergo significant CYP450 metabolism. Rifampicin's induction does not influence Lamivudine's effectiveness or safety, so dose adjustment is unnecessary.

  • Secondly before initiating drug therapy blood samples are taken to measure the baseline viral markers
  • Then, triple drug therapy is given which includes Tenofovir, Lamivudine and a boosted protease inhibitor for 28 days.
  • After 6 weeks again viral markers are measured to check for the infection.

question_text: Therapy with elvitegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir is initiated to 35-year-old woman with HIV-1. The physician also prescribes a new drug, cobicistat, which does not have antiretroviral activity. Which of the following is the most likely reason for prescribing cobicistat?

Cobicistat is a CYP3A4 inhibitor, not an antiretroviral drug. Both oral contraceptives and antiretroviral drugs are metabolized through CYP3A4.

question_text: A 43-year-old presents today complaining of a new rash on his chest and axilla, which you diagnose as tinea corporis.  He has a history of HIV, hypertension, coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, and ischemic cardiomyopathy. He is on antiretroviral therapy. You would like to prescribe a course of oral ketoconazole for therapy. You should consider dose adjustment for all of the following medicines that he is already taking EXCEPT:
explanation:
Carvedilol is metabolized by CYP2C19 and would not be affected by concomitant ketoconazole dosing.

Mexiletine, lovastatin and ritonavir, are all substrates of the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A4. As one of the most ubiquitous drug clearance enzymes, CYP3A4 metabolism is often a culprit in adverse drug–drug interactions, and the savvy clinician will be wary of co-prescribing drugs metabolized by this enzyme.

Ketoconazole is a powerful inhibitor of CYP3A4, and co-administration of ketoconazole with lovastatin, mexiletine, ritonavir, and saquinavir may lead to impressive increases in the plasma level of these medications, resulting in potential toxicity. In fact, the CYP3A4-inhibition qualities of ketoconazole are sometimes leveraged to increase drug levels of medications like tacrolimus in the post transplant patient when stable and elevated tacrolimus levels are required to prevent organ rejection.

question_text: In the case of a newborn delivered by an HIV-positive woman who was not receiving treatment, what is the recommended initial course of treatment to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV?
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the recommended initial course of treatment to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV is nevirapine + zidovudine + lamivudine for 6 weeks as the child is at high-risk of transmission.

Prevention of Parent-to-Child Transmission of HIV (PPTCT) guidelines:

Explanation of other options:

Nevirapine 6 months (Option A): Nevirapine is an antiretroviral drug used to reduce the risk of HIV transmission from mother to child. However, the standard prophylactic course for newborns is generally 6 weeks, not 6 months.

Zidovudine 6 weeks (Option B): Zidovudine is an antiretroviral agent given to lower the chance of HIV transmission from mother to infant. The usual newborn protocol includes a chance of HIV transmission from mother to infant. The usual newborn protocol includes a 6-week course, which, when used alongside other preventive strategies, effectively decreases the risk of transmission.

Nevirapine 6 weeks (Option D): Nevirapine is a widely used antiretroviral drug for infants at risk of acquiring HIV. The usual prophylactic duration is 6 weeks, and when included in a complete prevention approach, it helps lower the likelihood of transmission.

question_text:
Which of the following drugs acts by suicide inhibition?
1. Spironolactone
2. Ethinyl estradiol
3. Benzbromarone
4. Ritonavir
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Suicide inhibition refers to an irreversible form of enzyme inhibition in which a drug binds to an enzyme and forms a stable covalent complex, leading to permanent inactivation of that enzyme.
  • Ritonavir, an HIV protease inhibitor, exemplifies this mechanism by irreversibly inhibiting CYP3A4, a major enzyme in drug metabolism. This action increases the plasma concentrations of other drugs metabolized by CYP3A4.
  • Benzbromarone also acts via suicide inhibition, targeting the urate transporter in the kidneys to reduce uric acid reabsorption, thereby lowering serum urate levels in gout management.
  • Spironolactone: Along with eplerenone and finerenone, it functions as a competitive antagonist of aldosterone at mineralocorticoid receptors, rather than through suicide inhibition (Option A, B & D Ruled Out).
  • Ethinyl estradiol: A synthetic estrogen used in oral contraceptives, which does not act via suicide inhibition but exerts its effects by modulating estrogen receptors and feedback mechanisms on gonadotropins (Option A & B Ruled Out).

Key Takeaways:

  • Suicide inhibitors irreversibly bind enzymes.
  • Ritonavir → CYP3A4 inhibitor.
  • Benzbromarone → urate transporter inhibitor.

question_text: Which of the following drugs binds to CD4 and has both CXCR4 and CCR5 activity?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ibalizumab is a monoclonal antibody and post-attachment inhibitor that binds to the CD4 receptor and blocks HIV's interaction with both CCR5 and CXCR4 co-receptors, preventing viral entry into T cells.

Explanation of other options:

Maraviroc (Option A): Incorrect because it is a CCR5 antagonist, not a CD4-binding agent. It blocks only the CCR5 co-receptor, not CXCR4.

Dolutegravir (Option C): Incorrect because it is an integrase inhibitor, preventing integration of viral DNA into the host genome after entry.

Tenofovir (Option D): Incorrect because it is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that blocks reverse transcription of viral RNA, not entry.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ibalizumab → binds CD4, blocks CCR5 and CXCR4.
  • Maraviroc → CCR5 only.
  • Dolutegravir → integrase inhibitor.
  • Tenofovir → NRTI.

question_text: Which medication is effective for treating both HIV and Hepatitis B infections?
explanation:
Explanation:

Tenofovir is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) used to treat both HIV and Hepatitis B infections. It works by blocking the reverse transcriptase enzyme, which is crucial for the replication of both viruses.

Explanation for other options:

Dolutegravir (Option A): is an integrase inhibitor used to treat HIV but is not effective against Hepatitis B.

Zidovudine (Option C): is an NRTI that targets HIV reverse transcriptase but does not work against Hepatitis B, as it is not effective against the Hepatitis B reverse transcriptase enzyme.

Ritonavir (Option D): is a protease inhibitor used in HIV treatment, primarily to enhance the effects of other protease inhibitors by inhibiting CYP3A. However, it has no activity against Hepatitis B.

question_text: If a protease inhibitor-based antiretroviral regimen is used to treat his HIV, Then which of the following anti-tuberculosis drug should be avoided?

question_text: In the management of CMV retinitis, which among the following drugs is considered the drug of choice?
explanation:
Explanation:

The preferred treatment for CMV retinitis is ganciclovir which is formed from its prodrug valganciclovir.

Explanation of other options:

Cotrimoxazole (Option A): A combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, is widely used for treating different bacterial and certain opportunistic infections. However, it does not have activity against cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections.

Valacyclovir (Option B): An antiviral drug mainly prescribed for managing herpes simplex and herpes zoster infections. It lacks strong activity against CMV.

Tenofovir (Option C): An antiretroviral drug primarily used for managing and preventing HIV infection. Although it may show some activity against other viruses, it is not usually the preferred treatment for CMV retinitis, as agents like ganciclovir are more effective for this condition.

question_text: A 27-year-old woman comes with vomiting, urinary frequency, urgency, and burning on urination. Her temperature is 39.2°C and physical examination shows costovertebral angle pain. Her past history is significant for mild GERD for which she takes antacids several times per week. Treatment is begun. She returns 3 days later because of worsening urinary symptoms. Which of the following medications was the patient most likely prescribed?
explanation:
• The bacterial spectrum of uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women primarily consists mainly of E coli (75 to 95 %). Enterobacteriaceae, such as Proteus mirabilis and Klebsiella pneumonia, as well as the gram-positive Staphylococcus saprophyticus may also be found in a much smaller percentage of cases. This patient is presenting with the classical triad of pyelonephritis symptoms: fever, costovertebral angle pain, and nausea and/or vomiting.
  • Symptoms of cystitis may or may not be present to varying degrees and include urinary frequency, hesitancy, lower abdominal pain, and urgency.
  • Since the bacteria in most cases of community-acquired infections is usually E. coli or other Enterobacteriaceae, acceptable treatment regimens include fluoroquinolones (i.e., ciprofloxacin), cephalosporins, penicillins, extended-spectrum penicillins, carbapenems, and aminoglycosides. In this case, the physician likely prescribed the fluoroquinolone ciprofloxacin without paying attention to the drug interaction between this drug and antacids, which the patient is taking on a regular basis.
  • Fluoroquinolones, such as ciprofloxacin, will have a dramatic decrease in bioavailability when taken with antacids, secondary to the binding of the two medications in the intestinal tract. Thus, when taken with antacids, the fluoroquinolones will become ineffective and the patient's symptoms will continue to worsen. The concomitant use of antacids and fluoroquinolones is contraindicated, unless they are taken 2 hr before or 1hr after taking the drug.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 839

question_text: Among the following antibiotics, which agent is least likely to precipitate seizures in patients, including those with predisposing factors such as renal impairment or CNS disease?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Macrolides (e.g., azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) generally do not lower seizure threshold.
  • Main adverse effects: gastrointestinal disturbances (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain), QT prolongation, rare hepatotoxicity.
  • Seizures are extremely rare and not a significant clinical concern, making macrolides the safest in patients prone to CNS excitability.

Explanation of Other Options:

Beta-lactam compounds (Option A): Penicillins (especially high-dose penicillin G, piperacillin), cephalosporins (especially cefepime), and carbapenems (e.g., imipenem) can cross the blood-brain barrier and lower seizure threshold, especially in renal failure or CNS disease.

Quinolones (Option B): Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin can inhibit GABA receptors → increased risk of seizures, tremors, and CNS stimulation.

Isoniazid (Option D): Can cause seizures due to depletion of pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6), particularly in overdose or malnourished patients.

question_text: A 15 yr old female, complaints of cough and sore throat. She was prescribed an antibiotic, following which she came back with this symptom. Which drug would have caused it?
explanation:
Adverse effects of Penicillins

Penicillin G is one of the most nontoxic antibiotics; up to 20 MU has been injected in a day without any organ toxicity.

Local irritancy and direct toxicity Pain at i.m. injection site, nausea on oral ingestion and thrombophlebitis of injected vein are dose-related expressions of irritancy.

Accidental i.v. injection of procaine penicillin produces CNS stimulation, hallucinations and convulsions due to procaine.

question_text: A 34-year-old man with painless lesion on his penis presents with diffuse maculopapular rash involving the trunk, extremities, palms, and soles. RPR and FTA-ABS are positive. Next step in the management ?
option_c: IV Penicillin G weekly for 3 week
explanation:
let's explain each option:

A) Doxycycline:

  • Doxycycline is an antibiotic that can be used to treat syphilis, particularly in patients with a penicillin allergy.
  • It is typically used in cases of early syphilis or when penicillin is not an option due to allergies.
  • However, in patients without penicillin allergies and for the initial treatment of syphilis, penicillin is the preferred choice.

B) IM Penicillin G single dose:

  • This is the recommended treatment for early syphilis, which includes primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis.
  • It involves a single intramuscular injection of Penicillin G, and it is highly effective in curing syphilis at these stages.

C) IV Penicillin G weekly for 3 weeks:

  • This treatment regimen is typically used for late latent syphilis or tertiary syphilis, which are more advanced stages of the disease.
  • It involves intravenous administration of Penicillin G on a weekly basis for three weeks.
  • This extended treatment course is necessary to effectively treat the disease at this stage.

D) Desensitization:

  • Desensitization is a process used when a patient has a documented penicillin allergy but penicillin is the preferred treatment for syphilis.
  • It involves gradually exposing the patient to small, increasing doses of penicillin to desensitize their immune system and reduce the risk of an allergic reaction.
  • Once desensitization is successfully completed, the patient can receive penicillin for syphilis treatment.

In summary, for a patient with a positive RPR and FTA-ABS test indicating syphilis, the most appropriate next step is:

B) IM Penicillin G single dose

This is the standard and preferred treatment for early syphilis. Other options like doxycycline and IV Penicillin G are considered in specific situations, and desensitization is used for patients with penicillin allergies.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology, Fourteenth Edition By Bertram G. Katzung Pg no. 808

question_text: A nursing mother presented with fever and breast tenderness after two weeks postpartum, which oral antibiotics is ideal for her condition?
explanation:
Dicloxacillin

Oxacillin, cloxacillin and dicloxacillin are semisynthetic penicillin congeners that are markedly resistant to cleavage by penicillinase. These drugs are not substitutes for penicillin G in the treatment of diseases amenable to it and are not active against enterococci or Listeria. Oral administration is not a substitute for the parenteral routein the treatment of serious staphylococcal infections.

Pharmacological Properties. The isoxazolyl penicillins are potentinhibitors of the growth of most penicillinase-producing staphylococci.These agents are absorbed rapidly butincompletely (30%-80%) from the GI tract.

All these congeners are bound to plasma albumin to a great extent (~90%-95%); none is removed from the circulation to a significant degree by hemodialysis.

The half-lives for all are between 30 and 60 min. No dosing adjustments are needed for patients with renal failure.

question_text: A 26-year-old man presents with a single, painless ulcer on his penis. you want to treat him for syphilis with penicillin G, but his history includes an itchy rash following amoxicillin treatment as a child. What must first occur in the body for a penicillin to become allergenic?
option_a: First-pass metabolism in the liver creates a toxic metabolite
option_b: It must bind to a larger molecule, resulting in a complex that the body sees as a foreign antigen
option_c: Simple exposure to penicillin can cause sensitisation, which leads to a hypersensitivity reaction in sub- sequent exposures
option_d: Penicillin is not allergenic injection of penicillin simply causes histamine release by a mechanism not involving IgE
explanation:
It must bind to a larger molecule, resulting in a complex that the body sees as a foreign antigen. Although many patients inaccurately report an allergy to penicillin, a patient who developed urticaria following exposure to penicillin likely does have an allergy and should not be exposed again without being tested first. The penicillin molecule by itself is too small to be allergenic. According to the hapten hypothesis, such drugs likely bind to proteins or other macromolecules that the body then recognises as foreign.

A. The liver plays only a minor role in the elimination of penicillin. Most is excreted unchanged in the urine. The metabolites that are formed are not known to be particularly toxic.

C. This is not correct because penicillin itself does not cause an immune reaction. Only after binding to a macromolecule does penicillin become allergenic.

D. Morphine is an example of a drug that causes histamine release not involving immunoglobulin. This has not been demonstrated with penicillin.

Reference: Basic & Clinical Pharmacology by Bertram G. Katzung Fourteenth Edition Pg no. 798

Similarly, many strains of gonococci are resistant to tetracyclines. Alternative drugs for gonorrhoea include cefixime or azithromycin.
  • Option D : Meropenem is used as Last-resort drugs (used only in life-threatening infections or after other antibiotics have failed) because of the significant adverse effects. Used in Intraabdominal infections, infections caused by Enterobacter spp. and ESBL-producing gram-negative bacilli.

explanation:

question_text: Resistance of pneumococci to penicillin G is due to
option_c: Changes in chemical structure of target penicillin- binding proteins
option_d: Changes in the d-Ala-d-Ala building block of peptidoglycan precursor
explanation:
